Why Nigeria Continues to Attract Global Technology Investment- GITEX CEO
By Lukman Oladokun
Deputy Governor of Lagos State, Dr Kadir Obafemi Hamzat, has made a strong case for Lagos as Africa’s premier destination for technology investment, urging global investors, technology firms and innovators to establish long-term operations in the state and use it as a gateway into the continent’s rapidly expanding digital economy.
Speaking on behalf of Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu at GITEX Nigeria 2026 held at the Landmark Event Centre, Lagos, Hamzat said the state’s emergence as the host of one of the world’s leading technology exhibitions reflects its growing economic influence, innovation ecosystem and strategic importance to Africa’s future economy.
According to him, the decision to host GITEX in Lagos was not based on goodwill or sentiment, but on the city’s economic strength and growing relevance within the global technology landscape.
“It was not a courtesy extended to us. It was a commercial judgement made about Lagos,” Hamzat said. “We did not earn this event because Lagos is easy. Lagos is not easy. We earned it because Lagos is consequential. What happens in this city sets the direction for this continent.”
The Deputy Governor said Lagos has evolved into one of Africa’s most influential economic hubs, with developments in the state increasingly shaping technology, innovation and investment trends across the continent. He noted that startups founded in Lagos have grown into cross-border businesses operating in sectors such as financial technology, logistics and e-commerce, reinforcing the state’s reputation as a leading innovation ecosystem.
Highlighting infrastructure as a key driver of growth, Hamzat said Lagos has deployed about 3,000 kilometres of fibre-optic infrastructure and is progressing towards a 6,000-kilometre unified fibre network to expand broadband access and strengthen the digital economy. He stated that the network was built under an open-access model that enables operators to share infrastructure, thereby reducing costs and accelerating connectivity projects.
“When a new entrant arrives in Lagos, the most expensive part of their network is already on the ground,” he said. “Lagos is not at the end of the world’s digital infrastructure. Lagos is one of its landing points.”
Addressing concerns around power supply, Hamzat said Lagos has opted for structural reforms, including its Electricity Law, the establishment of the Lagos State Electricity Regulatory Commission and the licensing of operators across generation, distribution and metering. He added that the state is pursuing increased electricity capacity and expanded access to reliable power for businesses and residents.
“Lagos has constraints, but what distinguishes Lagos is that we name those constraints, we regulate them, we finance them and we invite you to build the solution with us,” he said.
The Deputy Governor identified talent as Lagos’ greatest competitive advantage, noting that technology professionals from the state are contributing to organisations across major innovation centres around the world. He also highlighted state-backed support for research, innovation and entrepreneurship through various initiatives aimed at strengthening the startup ecosystem and commercialising research outputs.
On artificial intelligence, Hamzat said Africa must play an active role in creating technologies rather than merely consuming them.
“We must become builders. That means talent, compute capacity, data infrastructure, research institutions and commercial models that keep value on this continent instead of exporting it,” he said.
In a direct appeal to international technology companies, he urged investors to deepen their presence in Lagos by establishing engineering hubs, data centres, research facilities and regional headquarters in the state.
“Do not merely sell into Lagos. Put your engineering here. Put your data centre capacity here. Put your regional headquarters here,” Hamzat added.
He said Lagos remains committed to building an innovation-driven economy where technology serves as a catalyst for growth, inclusion and prosperity.
“The future will not be built by those who predict it. It will be built by those who have the courage to create. And here in Lagos, we are creating,” he said.
Also speaking, the Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa, said Nigeria is strategically positioning itself as Africa’s digital innovation hub through investments in artificial intelligence, digital skills, sovereign digital infrastructure and emerging technologies.
Addressing government officials, technology leaders, investors and development partners, Inuwa said the global economy is undergoing a profound transformation in which intelligence, creativity and innovation are becoming the primary drivers of prosperity.
“Artificial Intelligence is making intelligence abundant and accessible. Countries that can effectively harness human creativity, innovation and digital capabilities will define the future global economy,” he said.
According to the NITDA Director-General, Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda aligns with the Federal Government’s economic diversification and growth strategy, with technology serving as a critical enabler of productivity, competitiveness and inclusive development
He said government is pursuing a comprehensive approach that combines talent development, innovation support, policy reform and strategic infrastructure investments to position Nigeria as a leading digital economy on the continent. This includes efforts to integrate digital literacy and emerging technology skills into the education system and expand initiatives such as the 3 Million Technical Talent programme.
Inuwa also highlighted the importance of advancing frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, robotics, additive manufacturing and the Internet of Things to improve productivity across agriculture, healthcare, education, manufacturing and public service delivery.
On digital sovereignty, he said Nigeria is implementing policies around data sovereignty, cloud sovereignty, operational sovereignty and AI sovereignty to ensure the country actively develops and owns digital solutions.
“We do not want to be at the receiving end of technology alone. We want to be active builders, creators and owners of technology that solves real problems and creates value for our people,” Inuwa said.
He further highlighted initiatives aimed at strengthening the innovation ecosystem, including implementation of the Startup Act, e-invoicing systems, public key infrastructure, software quality assurance standards and reforms to technology procurement processes. These measures, he said, are intended to create an enabling environment for startups and technology companies to scale and compete globally.
The NITDA boss also pointed out that investments in digital public infrastructure, broadband expansion and increased computing capacity as essential foundations for a thriving digital economy
Calling for deeper collaboration, he invited global technology companies, investors and ecosystem partners to work with Nigeria in developing solutions for Africa and international markets.
“Nigeria is open for innovation, open for partnership and open for investment. We invite the world to come and build with us as we shape the future of digital transformation in Africa,” he said.
He noted that GITEX Nigeria 2026 provides an important platform for attracting investment, strengthening partnerships and showcasing Nigeria’s growing influence in the global digital economy. With the right combination of talent, innovation, policy support and infrastructure, he maintained that Nigeria is well-positioned to emerge as Africa’s leading digital innovation hub.
Earlier, Chief Executive Officer of GITEX, Trixie LohMirmand, said the decision to bring the global technology exhibition to Nigeria was based on clear evidence that the country is emerging as one of the world’s most dynamic centres for innovation, entrepreneurship and technology investment.
LohMirmand said the country’s progress since the inaugural event had been significant. She said, “A year ago when we stood here, all the conversations were about the potential of Nigeria and Lagos. Today, Lagos is the highest-rated startup ecosystem and ranks number one in Africa for AI activity and funding,” she said.
She noted that Nigeria’s artificial intelligence strategy had advanced from policy development to implementation, helping to strengthen the country’s attractiveness to investors seeking talent, innovation and growth opportunities.
However, she said the next challenge is to translate that momentum into globally competitive businesses, exports and jobs.
“The challenge now is about turning those advantages into globally competitive businesses, exports, jobs and knowledge. Talent needs access to markets. Startups need access to customers. Innovation needs capital, and capital needs confidence,” LohMirmand said.
She explained that GITEX serves as a bridge connecting Nigerian innovators and entrepreneurs with international investors, technology leaders and new markets.
“Nigeria has one of the biggest assets in the world: its young people,” she said, stressing that technology events must move beyond showcasing startups to helping them build sustainable and globally competitive enterprises.
“It is not enough to consume AI. When you create AI, you become a superpower,” she added.
Describing the exhibition as more than a technology showcase, LohMirmand said GITEX functions as an economic platform that accelerates growth across the innovation ecosystem.
“Gitex is not an exhibition. It is an economic infrastructure that supports the technology ecosystem,” she said.
She added that the event compresses years of networking, partnership building and business development into a few days by bringing together investors, multinational technology companies, policymakers and innovators from across the world.
LohMirmand concluded that the success of GITEX Nigeria demonstrates that the country is no longer simply a market to watch but an increasingly important player in the global innovation economy.
“For us, the mission is clear. We are bringing the world into Nigeria and creating the connections that help Nigerian innovation reach the rest of the world,” she said.

items.content:
By Lukman Oladokun
The Director General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa, has reiterated the Federal Government’s commitment to building a private sector-driven, government-enabled digital economy, describing technology as the cornerstone of Nigeria’s ambition to become a trillion-dollar economy.
Reacting to responses from Rhett Power, a Forbe USA columnist on the theme “The Nigeria First Approach to Building Digital Sovereignty” during a fireside chat at GITEX 2026 in Lagos, Inuwa said President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has been serving as Nigeria’s “Chief Marketing Officer” by creating an enabling environment for businesses to thrive and attract investment into the country’s digital ecosystem.
According to him, digital transformation is no longer optional for economic growth. “Today, you cannot talk about business or the economy without talking about digital technology. If we are serious about building a trillion-dollar economy, digital technology will play a critical role. Technology is a powerful tool that can help organisations and individuals achieve two, three or even ten times more productivity, leading to greater prosperity and wealth creation across the country,’’ he said.
The NITDA boss noted that while digital technologies present enormous opportunities, Nigeria must also ensure it has control over the infrastructure that powers the digital economy.
He explained that value creation in the digital age depends heavily on data, connectivity and computing power. However, without adequate control over how data is collected, stored, processed and governed, nations may struggle to fully realise the benefits of technological advancement.
To address this challenge, he highlighted the Federal Government’s National Cloud First Policy, which encourages government institutions and large organisations to prioritise cloud adoption when deploying digital solutions.
“Building and maintaining digital infrastructure is expensive. There are operational costs, technology refresh cycles and significant investment requirements,” Inuwa said. “Cloud adoption allows organisations to focus more on innovation and service delivery rather than spending resources managing infrastructure.”
He stressed that the policy is not designed to exclude global technology companies or create barriers to international investment. “Contrary to suggestions that it could be protectionist, the policy is the exact opposite. We are inviting hyperscalers and major technology companies to come to Nigeria, invest in Nigeria, build with us and operate in line with our laws and regulations while utilising Nigerian talent.”
According to him, Nigeria’s vision for digital sovereignty extends beyond hosting data locally. It also includes ensuring Nigerians participate actively in building, managing and operating digital services and infrastructure.
“We want our people to acquire the skills and capabilities needed to build and run these services. We want these services developed within our jurisdiction and in accordance with Nigerian laws,” he said.
Inuwa clarified that the policy does not prohibit the use of public cloud services. Rather, it introduces a classification framework that recognises certain categories of information as sovereign data requiring stronger protection.
He identified defence-related information, financial transaction records, healthcare information and citizens’ personal data as strategic assets that should remain within Nigeria’s borders for reasons of national security, economic stability and citizen protection.
“There are technologies that allow organisations to process workloads on public cloud platforms while ensuring sensitive data remains stored within the country,” he noted.
The NITDA Director General further argued that the policy is already creating a stronger investment case for data centre operators and digital infrastructure developers. By providing clear regulatory direction, investors can have greater confidence that their infrastructure will attract users and generate value.
Inuwa observed that Nigeria has historically served as a major gateway for internet connectivity across the region. As local computing capacity expands, he said the country is strategically placed to provide digital services and infrastructure to neighbouring countries, particularly landlocked nations seeking access to reliable cloud and computing resources.
Addressing the issue of coordination across different levels of government, Inuwa said NITDA continues to work closely with state governments to align digital policies and regulatory frameworks.
“Our mandate is national, but we collaborate extensively with states to ensure digital transformation reaches every part of the country,” he explained. According to him, President Tinubu’s broader vision is centred on national prosperity and inclusivity, ensuring that no state is left behind in Nigeria’s digital journey.
“In any network, you are only as strong as your weakest link,” he said. “That is why the vision is to ensure every state is connected, every state has the right policies, and every state develops its own digital talent capable of building solutions that can scale nationally.”
Speaking directly to entrepreneurs attending the conference, Inuwa highlighted the government’s growing efforts to create opportunities for startups beyond the fintech sector.
He pointed to Nigeria’s success in financial technology as evidence of how deliberate government policies can unlock innovation. According to him, the Central Bank of Nigeria’s cashless policy created the conditions that enabled the country’s fintech ecosystem to flourish and produce globally recognised companies.
Building on that model, he said the government is now extending digital transformation to other critical sectors citing the recent establishment of the National Health Technology Office, which is expected to accelerate the digitalisation of healthcare services and create new opportunities for health-tech innovators.
“We are doing the same thing in agriculture, education and other sectors,” he said. “These are opportunities for entrepreneurs to identify challenges and use technology to build innovative solutions.”
Inuwa encouraged Nigerian startups to embrace disruptive thinking and create entirely new business models capable of transforming industries, drawing parallels with how companies such as Uber redefined transportation through technology.
“What the President wants is not business as usual. He wants Nigerians to harness the power of technology to create new value propositions and solve real problems. We want to see startups building the next generation of solutions across health-tech, agri-tech, ed-tech and many other sectors.”
He reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to creating an environment where innovation, investment and digital talent can thrive, positioning Nigeria as a leading technology hub on the African continent.

By Lukman Oladokun
At the sideline of the GITEX Nigeria, the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA) have entered into a strategic partnership aimed at accelerating Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda, fostering innovation, and empowering businesses across the country through technology-driven growth.
The partnership was formalised through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) by the Director General of NITDA, Kashifu Inuwa and the Director General of NACCIMA, Engr. Olusola Obadimu marking a significant milestone in the nation’s journey towards building an inclusive and competitive digital economy.
Speaking shortly after the signing ceremony, the Director General of NACCIMA described the agreement as a timely and strategic intervention for the private sector, emphasizing that digital transformation has become imperative for businesses seeking relevance and competitiveness in today’s global economy.
“It is an excellent arrangement to have this type of protocol on digitisation and digital transformation, especially for the private sector,” he said. “NACCIMA is the umbrella body of the organised private sector in Nigeria, and digital transformation is a necessity. There is no better partner to work with than NITDA, and we are happy to sign this MoU and move the partnership forward.”
The agreement provides a structured framework for collaboration in several key areas, including the development of a collaborative digital ecosystem platform, enterprise digital transformation for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promotion of digital innovation and technology adoption, capacity building for Nigerian businesses, and strategic cooperation towards the successful development and institutionalisation of the Digital Nigeria International Conference (DNICE) 2026 and subsequent editions.
The partnership also seeks to facilitate stronger linkages among government institutions, private sector organisations, technology companies, academia, investors, development partners, and other stakeholders, creating an enabling environment for innovation and economic growth.
 
Underscoring the urgency of implementation, the NACCIMA DG disclosed that both organisations are prepared to commence execution of the agreement immediately.
“We are going to hit the ground running as soon as we return to our offices for the implementation of this agreement. Nigerians will begin to see things happen almost instantaneously,” he stated.
According to the NACCIMA DG, the partnership holds immense prospects for Nigeria, particularly for the country’s growing youth population, who are increasingly driving innovation and digital entrepreneurship.
“Digitalisation is the way to go. As you can see, we have a youthful population, and they are the ones driving this process. We should encourage them and give them all the necessary support to go beyond Nigeria and compete on the global stage,” he said.
The collaboration aligns with NITDA’s broader mandate of driving Nigeria’s digital economy through technology innovation, digital literacy, and business transformation, while leveraging NACCIMA’s extensive network and influence across the organised private sector.

items.content:
No fewer than 200 young Nigerians have been equipped with critical digital and innovation skills through the NITDA Summer Training Programme and Free Long Vacation Young School Kids Coding Bootcamp tagged IoT and Scratch Programming held at the Federal Technical College (FTC), Yaba, Lagos.
The initiative, organised by the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) in collaboration with Cisco and UNITeS Academy, provided participants with hands-on exposure to emerging technologies and digital competencies designed to prepare them for the future of work and innovation.
During the intensive training programme, the students gained practical knowledge in coding, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), robotics, programming, game development, animation and digital creativity. Beyond technical skills, the bootcamp also strengthened their problem-solving, critical thinking, collaboration and computational thinking abilities, empowering them to become active creators of technology rather than passive consumers.
Speaking at the closing ceremony, NITDA’s Director-General, represented by the Director of the South-West Zonal Office, described the programme as more than a holiday learning initiative, noting that it was a strategic investment in Nigeria’s digital future.
He commended the participants for their enthusiasm, creativity and determination throughout the programme, urging them to sustain the momentum by continuing to learn, innovate and develop solutions to real-world challenges.
“The end of this bootcamp marks the beginning of a much longer journey. The children before us today are potential software developers, Artificial Intelligence specialists, cybersecurity experts, robotics engineers and digital entrepreneurs who can shape Nigeria’s digital economy,” he said.
The Director-General also called on parents, guardians, schools and other stakeholders to support continuous digital learning by encouraging responsible technology use, strengthening coding clubs and creating more opportunities for practical innovation.
The Federal Technical College, Yaba, also lauded NITDA, Cisco and UNITeS Academy for investing in the next generation of innovators. Speaking on behalf of the Principal, Mrs A.O. Ajayi, the College’s representative described the programme as a timely intervention that aligns with the growing need to develop technologically skilled young people capable of thriving in a rapidly evolving digital world.
According to the College, the initiative demonstrates the importance of exposing children to science, technology and innovation at an early age, enabling them to build confidence, creativity and practical skills that can contribute to national development.
The institution encouraged the participants to remain curious, continue exploring new ideas and leverage technology to address societal challenges. It further emphasised that education should extend beyond the classroom to include innovation, creativity and the practical application of knowledge.
FTC Yaba also expressed appreciation to parents and guardians for their support throughout the programme and reaffirmed its commitment to nurturing young Nigerians through quality technical, vocational, scientific and technological education.
The success of the training programme underscores the growing impact of collaborative efforts between government, educational institutions and private-sector partners in building Nigeria’s digital talent pipeline. By equipping 200 young learners with future-ready skills and exposing them to emerging technologies, the initiative has laid a foundation for a new generation of digital creators, innovators and technology leaders.
As the participants received their certificates at the close of the programme, the message from organisers and stakeholders was clear: the journey has just begun. The knowledge, skills and confidence gained during the bootcamp have the potential to shape careers, inspire innovation and contribute meaningfully to Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda.
Some of the participants described the bootcamp as a life-changing experience that expanded their understanding of technology and inspired them to pursue careers in the digital sector.
The senior category’s winner, Ayodele Easther PipeOluwa said, “Before attending the bootcamp, I only used computers for basic tasks. Now, I understand coding and how technology can be used to solve problems. I want to become a software developer in the future.”
Another student, Jonathan Chukwumah expressed excitement about learning robotics and Artificial Intelligence, noting that the programme had increased her confidence and encouraged her to explore innovative ideas.
Parents also praised the initiative for exposing their children to practical digital skills during the holiday period. According to one of the parents, Mrs. Omole A. Oluwunmi she disclosed that the bootcamp helped their children develop creativity, discipline and a stronger interest in technology.
For many of the participants, the training was more than just a holiday activity. It served as a gateway to new opportunities, inspiring them to dream bigger and positioning them to become future innovators capable of contributing to Nigeria’s growing digital economy.

By Naeemah Junaid
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has expressed readiness to strengthen collaboration with the Centre for Inclusive Development (CID) to promote digital accessibility and ensure that persons with disabilities are not excluded from Nigeria’s digital transformation.
The commitment was made when CID paid a courtesy visit to NITDA to present findings from its research on digital accessibility for persons with disabilities and explore opportunities for stronger standards and greater inclusion in Nigeria’s digital ecosystem.
Representing the Director General of NITDA, Dr Ayodeji Eniola, Director, Corporate Planning and Strategy, said the findings were consistent with the Agency’s mandate of ensuring that no Nigerian is left behind in the country’s digital transformation.
Inuwa said NITDA’s digital literacy drive, which targets 70 per cent digital literacy nationwide by 2027, was being implemented across schools, the informal sector and the workforce.
He said the Agency was particularly interested in ensuring that digital skills and access were extended to Nigerians irrespective of their status.
The DG noted that the Agency will be interested in working with CID to ensure that it deepens ongoing efforts to ensure that digital skills are effectively cascaded to all Nigerians, irrespective of their status.
Inuwa said there was need for stronger measures to ensure that digital technologies serve every Nigerian.
The DG added that NITDA had already identified gaps relating to persons with disabilities in its digital literacy framework and commenced efforts to address them.
He disclosed that the development of national accessibility standards was among the issues the Agency would seek to advance, while noting that accessibility considerations had already been incorporated into NITDA’s revised website guidelines for government institutions.
Inuwa reaffirmed the Agency’s willingness to deepen collaboration with the Centre, particularly in the areas of digital literacy and accessibility.
The engagement underscored the growing need for accessibility to remain a central component of Nigeria’s digital transformation, with both organisations expressing readiness to explore practical measures that will enable persons with disabilities to participate more independently and securely in the digital economy.
Presenting the research findings, Ms Tracy Onabis Agbamu, Nigerian disability rights advocate, lawyer and researcher, disclosed that the study audited about 30 government digital platforms, with only 47 per cent meeting the required accessibility threshold.
She, however, identified NITDA among the platforms that performed strongly in the assessment, attributing the performance to the Agency’s efforts towards digital inclusion.
The study also uncovered considerable accessibility challenges on private-sector platforms, particularly in the banking, fintech and payment sectors.
According to her, such barriers could compel persons with disabilities to depend on third parties to access digital financial services, potentially exposing them to privacy and security risks.
Agbamu noted that digital inclusion goes beyond equipping citizens with digital skills, stressing that digital platforms must also be designed to support assistive technologies and independent access.
To address the identified gaps, Agbamu called for NITDA’s intervention in developing guidance on accessibility statements for government websites, integrating accessibility requirements into procurement and licensing frameworks, and promoting accessibility standards across critical sectors.
It also sought NITDA’s technical support for the development and validation of a national digital accessibility standard for Nigeria.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
…prove my Ekiti origin claim or face legal action
…we welcome the lawsuit — Hunye
By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta
The Ogun State governorship candidate of the All Progressives Congress, APC, Senator Solomon Adeola, has given Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, chieftain, Abayomi Hunye, and Ambassador Folake Marcus-Bello 24 hours to produce evidence to substantiate their claims that he is of Ekiti State origin or face legal action.
Adeola issued the ultimatum through his Media Adviser, Chief Kayode Odunaro, following separate appearances by Hunye and Marcus-Bello on programmes aired by Channels Television.
According to a statement by Odunaro, the two politicians allegedly claimed during their television appearances that Adeola was originally from Ekiti State, among other allegations, without providing evidence to substantiate the claims.
Adeola described the allegations as false and defamatory, challenging his accusers to produce documentary evidence to support their claims.
“I watched in utter disbelief as these characters that I hardly know utter assertive and outrageous lies about my origin without any proof,” Adeola said.
“One falsely claimed on TV that I am from Ekiti and, when asked where exactly in Ekiti, went blank and could not provide an answer.
“The other one was lying about the locations of the graves of my parents as if she was part of the undertakers at the burial, all in a futile effort to justify an unsustainable falsehood.
“Enough is enough. They should produce their evidence in 24 hours or be ready for my lawsuits,” he added.
Adeola’s camp alleged that claims about his purported Ekiti origin had previously been deployed as a political campaign strategy to frustrate his emergence as senator representing Ogun West Senatorial District.
The statement said the allegations did not stop Adeola from winning the 2023 National Assembly election, adding that he secured what it described as massive support from voters across the senatorial district.
It further alleged that the controversy had resurfaced against the backdrop of Adeola’s ambition to contest the 2027 Ogun State governorship election on the APC platform.
Odunaro maintained that the latest allegations were part of an attempt to undermine Adeola’s political aspiration ahead of the election.
However, Hunye welcomed Adeola’s threat of legal action, saying he was prepared to meet the senator in court and had documentary evidence to support his position.
In a statement issued through his Media Adviser, Femi Oyewale, Hunye said the threat of a lawsuit was welcome, while alleging that the issue concerning Adeola’s ancestry was already before a court.
“We are more than ready to meet Senator Adeola in a court of competent jurisdiction,” Hunye said.
“Interestingly, it seems they are not well informed that the matter is already in court. Threatening us with a lawsuit, therefore, is like a political jamboree designed to make noise in the public.”
Hunye accused Adeola’s camp of attempting to intimidate critics and divert attention from questions surrounding the senator’s ancestry and eligibility to govern Ogun State.
“For far too long, the political space in Ogun West has been subjected to intimidation, high-handedness, and the suppression of truth through propaganda and sponsored brickbats,” he alleged.
He argued that questions surrounding a political candidate’s origin and eligibility were matters of public interest rather than private issues.
“The issue of a candidate’s origin and eligibility is a matter of constitutional concern, not a private affair,” Hunye said.
“It touches on the integrity of our democratic institutions and the aspirations of the good people of Ogun State, who deserve a leader whose roots and allegiance are indisputably local.”
Hunye also maintained that truth would constitute a defence against a libel action, urging Adeola to approach the court if he believed the allegations were defamatory.
“We wish to remind the Senator and his media handlers that truth is an absolute defence against libel,” he said.
“Rather than engaging in empty threats and grandstanding on national television, Senator Adeola should save his energy and approach the court immediately.”
Hunye said he would not be intimidated by the threat of litigation, promising to present what he described as “robust, verifiable facts and documentary evidence” to substantiate the claims concerning Adeola’s alleged Ekiti ancestry.
“The courtroom is where evidence is tested, not the pages of newspapers or sponsored broadcast interviews,” he said.

items.content:
Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Lagos State, has questioned the eligibility of Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat to contest the 2027 governorship election, citing his alleged oath of allegiance to the United States.
Rhodes-Vivour raised the issue on Tuesday while appearing on Channels Television’s Sunrise Daily, recalling the controversy surrounding Hamzat’s eligibility during the 2023 governorship election.
He said his legal team had relied on the alleged US oath while challenging Hamzat’s qualification, arguing that a Nigerian public office holder should not simultaneously owe allegiance to another country.
“We focused on the fact that this current person that wants to contest for governor, deputy governor, swore an oath of allegiance to another country,” Rhodes-Vivour said.
“Constitutionally, that is one of the number one reasons to dismiss a candidate or dismiss somebody that emerges as the governor.”
During the 2023 election petition proceedings, Olubusayo Fasidi, an immigration lawyer, had testified before the Lagos State Governorship Election Petition Tribunal that Hamzat applied for US naturalisation and took an oath of allegiance to the country.
Fasidi, however, told the tribunal that she was invited to explain US immigration law and was not familiar with Nigeria’s constitutional provisions on dual citizenship.
Rhodes-Vivour also criticised the conduct of the 2023 election, alleging incidents of violence and intimidation across the state.
He said Nigerians should elect public officials whose loyalty is exclusively to the country.
The ADC candidate further argued that Hamzat could have publicly renounced any alleged US allegiance before seeking elective office, citing former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson as an example.
Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubu has endorsed Hamzat as the APC candidate for the Lagos governorship election.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Elizabeth Osayande
LAGOS — The Lagos State University branch of the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU-LASU) has declared a total and indefinite strike over what it described as the failure of the government to implement the 2025 ASUU/FGN Agreement.
The union announced the decision on Tuesday, September 15, following a congress at which members resolved to commence the industrial action.
In a statement signed by the Secretary of the ASUU-LASU Steering Committee, Comrade Thanny Nooem, and the Coordinator, Comrade Oluwaseun Babalola, the union said the decision followed months of what it described as “patient and constructive engagement” with the government without a resolution of the issues in dispute.
“This unfortunate and avoidable action has become necessary due to the continued failure of the Government to address the Union’s longstanding agitation over the implementation of the 2025 ASUU/FGN Agreement,” the statement said.
ASUU-LASU said it was seeking the “full domestication and implementation of the 2025 ASUU/FGN Agreement” as a condition for resolving the dispute.
“The strike shall be total and comprehensive until there is a satisfactory resolution of the issues in dispute,” the union said.
The union expressed regret over the development, saying previous efforts to resolve the matter through engagement had not produced the desired outcome.
The industrial action is expected to affect teaching and other academic activities at Lagos State University, including its Ojo campus and other campuses, pending further developments.
The union ended its statement with the slogan: “Aluta continua, victoria ascerta.”

According to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), graduate students accounted for 21% of new study permits issued from January to June 2026, up from 12% during the same period last year.

At the same time, the share of new study permit holders attending universities increased from 30% in 2024 to 40% in 2025, reflecting a stronger focus on higher-level education.
Most graduate degree students can benefit from simpler processing, while doctoral applicants may have their study permit applications processed within two weeks.
Eligible master’s and doctoral students studying at public institutions have also been exempt from the provincial or territorial attestation letter requirement since January 1, 2026.
Graduate students may also be able to bring eligible family members with them to Canada during their studies.
After completing their degrees, international graduates may qualify for a post-graduation work permit, allowing them to gain work experience in the country.
The Canadian government said it is looking to attract the world’s best and brightest researchers and graduate students as it gives greater priority to master’s and doctoral programs.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
New Zealand has announced a new six-month work visa for eligible international graduates who do not qualify for the country’s existing Post-Study Work Visa.
Applications for the Short-Term Graduate Work Visa will open on November 16, 2026. The visa will provide open work rights, allowing eligible graduates to work for any employer in New Zealand without needing a job offer before applying.
To qualify, applicants must have completed a New Zealand Qualifications and Credentials Framework Level 5, 6, or 7 qualification in New Zealand. The qualification must have been studied full-time for at least 24 weeks and must not already make the graduate eligible for a Post-Study Work Visa.
English-language, foundation, and bridging qualifications will not be eligible.
Applicants must also have at least NZ$5,000 to support themselves and meet New Zealand’s health and character requirements. Applications must be submitted within three months after the applicant’s student visa expires.
The visa can only be granted once and cannot be extended or renewed. It is intended to give graduates additional time to find employment and, if eligible, move to another work visa.
Visa holders will not be allowed to own or operate a business, and any work must be carried out under an employment agreement or a contract for services.
New Zealand is also expanding eligibility for its Post-Study Work Visa from November 16.
Under the revised rules, graduates who complete an eligible Level 7 Graduate Diploma in New Zealand may qualify for a Post-Study Work Visa if they already hold a bachelor’s degree from New Zealand or overseas.
The Graduate Diploma must be studied full-time in New Zealand for its entire duration, while cross-crediting or recognition of prior learning will not count toward the required study period.
The Post-Study Work Visa can allow eligible graduates to work in New Zealand for up to three years, depending on their qualification.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
The Himalayas are nearing a critical tipping point as glaciers melt faster than they did a decade ago, raising serious concerns over future water security across the region, according to a study released this month.
The region is also moving toward “peak water” by mid-century, the point at which river flows stop increasing and begin to decline.
The warning comes after the collapse of a Himalayan glacier along the Nepal-Tibet border in late August, which triggered landslides and flash floods in nearby valleys. At least 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, while more than 5,300 remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region.
The study found that retreating glaciers are leaving behind unstable glacial lakes, many of which are held back by loose rock and ice. These lakes are located above valleys where millions of people live, increasing the risk to downstream communities.
The research was produced by sustainability advisory firm Systemiq in collaboration with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, and India’s GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment.
According to the study, glacier mass loss across the Himalayas has accelerated in recent decades. However, only 21 glaciers are currently monitored on the ground out of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region.
The Hindu Kush-Himalaya stretches across eight countries, from Afghanistan to Myanmar.
In India alone, nearly 200 glacial lakes have been identified as high risk, including 56 classified as “very high risk,” leaving millions of people downstream exposed to potential disasters.
The study warned that the approach toward peak water could have major consequences for regional water security as river flows eventually begin to decline.
The Himalayas also hold major economic importance for India, supporting more than 20 percent of the country’s GDP and forming a key part of its national economic infrastructure. Hundreds of millions of people depend on the region.
Although the Himalayan region covers around 18 percent of India’s land area, it accounts for roughly 35 percent of the country’s natural disasters.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
A new study has linked the use of prescription weight-loss drugs with higher rates of depression and suicidal thoughts, with researchers finding an even stronger association among people who regained weight after treatment.
Researchers at Asan Medical Center in South Korea analyzed data from 27,741 adults who participated in the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey between 2013 and 2022. The participants included 10,908 men and 16,833 women.
Of the total, 846 participants reported taking medication prescribed by a doctor for weight control during the previous year, while 26,895 had not used weight-loss drugs. The study did not distinguish between different types of weight-loss medication.
The findings showed that 22.1% of weight-loss drug users reported experiencing depressive feelings for at least two consecutive weeks, compared with 11.4% of people who did not use the medications.
Suicidal thoughts were reported by 9.9% of users compared with 4.5% of non-users. Meanwhile, 2.2% of users reported making suicide plans compared with 1.4% of non-users, while suicide attempts were reported by 1.7% of users and 0.6% of non-users.
After accounting for other factors, researchers found that weight-loss medication users had 93% higher odds of depression and 168% higher odds of suicidal thoughts compared with non-users. They were also around twice as likely to seek counseling for mental health problems.
The association was particularly strong among people who gained weight after using the medication. In this group, the odds of suicidal thoughts were around 4.2 times higher than among people who did not use weight-loss drugs. They also had 1.9 times higher odds of depression and 1.8 times higher odds of seeking mental health counseling.
Researchers said the increase in depression and suicide-related indicators following weight regain could be linked to several factors. These may include possible neuropsychiatric effects of the medications as well as psychological and social stress associated with unsuccessful weight control or regaining weight after treatment.
The study, titled Association of Weight-Loss Medication Use and Weight Change with Depression and Suicidal Ideation and Behaviors, was published in the Korean Journal of Family Practice. However, the findings show an association and do not establish that weight-loss drugs directly cause depression or suicidal behavior.
Concerns over suicidal thoughts associated with weight-loss drugs have previously prompted reviews by health regulators. The US Food and Drug Administration began investigating reports involving GLP-1 drugs in 2023.
However, the FDA said in January 2026 that a comprehensive review of clinical trials, observational studies, and post-marketing data found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior associated with GLP-1 drugs. It subsequently asked manufacturers to remove the warning about suicidal behavior and ideation from the prescribing information for Wegovy, Saxenda, and Zepbound.

items.title: Punjab Launches Crackdown on Pressure Horns and Excessive Honking
items.summary:
The Punjab Traffic Police has ordered a province-wide crackdown on pressure horns and excessive honking, with a strict ban on the use of pressure horns taking effect across Punjab.
The Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Traffic has directed all Chief Traffic Officers (CTOs) and District Traffic Officers (DTOs) to take indiscriminate action against motorists found using pressure horns.
Traffic authorities have also been instructed to act against unnecessary honking near hospitals, educational institutions, emergency centers, and restricted zones. Motorists who continuously or repeatedly use their horns will also face action under the law.
Commercial vehicle owners have been told to immediately remove pressure horns from their vehicles or face legal action.
According to official data, more than 383,000 people have been fined across Punjab this year for using pressure horns and continuous honking. Lahore Traffic Police alone has issued challans to 48,000 people over the improper use of horns.

items.content:
The Punjab Traffic Police has ordered a province-wide crackdown on pressure horns and excessive honking, with a strict ban on the use of pressure horns taking effect across Punjab.
The Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Traffic has directed all Chief Traffic Officers (CTOs) and District Traffic Officers (DTOs) to take indiscriminate action against motorists found using pressure horns.
Traffic authorities have also been instructed to act against unnecessary honking near hospitals, educational institutions, emergency centers, and restricted zones. Motorists who continuously or repeatedly use their horns will also face action under the law.
Commercial vehicle owners have been told to immediately remove pressure horns from their vehicles or face legal action.
According to official data, more than 383,000 people have been fined across Punjab this year for using pressure horns and continuous honking. Lahore Traffic Police alone has issued challans to 48,000 people over the improper use of horns.
Authorities said pressure horns and continuous honking can harm human hearing and neurological health. The ongoing crackdown has also helped reduce noise pollution, according to the traffic authorities.
The DIG Traffic has directed officials to ensure effective enforcement to protect citizens from unnecessary noise and noise pollution while taking action against violators without discrimination.
Citizens have also been urged to cooperate with the traffic police in reducing noise pollution. Authorities said safe driving requires roads that are safe, peaceful, and environmentally friendly.

items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
India’s ubiquitous UPI payment system is set for a significant change from October 15, with the introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select transactions.
Under the new framework, merchants will be charged an MDR of 0.4% on person to merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The charge will be capped at ₹300 for transactions worth ₹75,000 or more.
The October 15 change does not necessarily make UPI a paid service for consumers. Instead, it introduces a commercial layer on the merchant side. With a 0.4% MDR for regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000 and a ₹300 cap for transactions of ₹75,000 and above.
The framework keeps P2P payments free, protects P2PM merchants from MDR and provides lower flat rates for sectors such as fuel, insurance and utilities.
The broader shift is from an entirely zero-MDR merchant model towards a threshold-based system intended to create a more sustainable financial model for India’s UPI infrastructure.
Payments Council of India’s chairman and AvenuesAI CEO Vishwas Patel believes that the introduction of the charges is a key step to build a viable economic model while keeping UPI free for consumers.
“At the same time, sustainability must not come at the cost of financial inclusion. The continued zero-MDR protection for eligible small and micro merchants, along with support for expanding digital acceptance in Tier III, IV centres, will help preserve UPI’s accessibility,” Patel said.
So, what exactly changes next month and who will actually have to pay?
UPI MDR: What Is Changing From October 15?
The new MDR framework will come into effect on October 15, 2026.
For regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000, merchants will pay 0.4% of the transaction value as MDR. Transactions of ₹2,000 or below will continue to attract zero MDR.
For high-value payments, the MDR will be capped at ₹300. This cap applies to transactions of ₹75,000 and above.
In practical terms, the structure will look like this:
Transaction value ₹2,000 – ₹0 MDR
Transaction value ₹3,000 – ₹12 MDR
Transaction value ₹50,000 – ₹200 MDR
Transaction value ₹75,000 – ₹300 MDR
Transaction value ₹1 Lakh – ₹300 MDR
The MDR is a charge on the merchant side. Consumers will continue to pay the listed price of the product or service.
P2P transactions, including transfers to friends, family or between a user’s own bank accounts, will continue to remain free.
UPI apps won’t be allowed to charge a platform fee or any other fee for payments made through UPI.
There are also no monthly quotas under the framework that would result in consumers being charged after a certain number of UPI transactions.
The new MDR is a merchant-side charge and not a consumer-facing UPI fee. Merchants onboarded under the framework cannot pass the MDR on to customers while accepting UPI payments, the NPCI said.
What About Small Merchants?
Not every merchant will be subject to the 0.4% MDR.
Small merchants operating under the Person-to-Person-Merchant (P2PM) framework will continue to enjoy zero MDR. The framework defines these as small vendors receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes directly into their accounts.
This means a small vendor does not automatically become liable for MDR simply because a customer makes a payment exceeding ₹2,000.
Acquiring banks and payment service providers will monitor the monthly inward transaction threshold. Merchants receiving more than ₹1 Lakh through UPI for three consecutive months will be transitioned to the P2M category, effectively making the
Existing QR codes will continue to work and small merchants will not have to replace their QR stands or soundboxes because of the MDR changes.
How Are MDR Charges Bifurcated Among Sectors?
Several sectors will not be charged the standard 0.4% MDR. Instead, they will have a flat MDR of ₹5 for transactions above ₹2,000.
These include categories such as railways, telecom, insurance and fuel.
For example, an insurance premium or fuel payment of ₹10,000 would attract a ₹5 MDR rather than the ₹40 charge that would apply under the standard 0.4% rate.
Utility payments, including electricity, water and piped natural gas, will also fall under the designated industry programme category, with a ₹5 MDR for transactions above ₹2,000.
Payments below ₹2,000 in these categories will continue to remain free of MDR.
What About Mutual Funds And Stock Market Payments?
Capital market transactions will have a separate MDR structure.
Payments involving mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers and dealers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, with a maximum cap of ₹300.
The category covers regulated capital-market entities, including asset management companies, SEBI-registered stockbrokers, securities dealers and investment platforms.
The lower rate is intended to distinguish investment-related payments from routine retail and commercial transactions.
Will Credit Card Payments On UPI Be Affected?
The new MDR framework applies specifically to direct account-to-merchant UPI payments.
Credit-linked UPI transactions, such as payments made using RuPay credit cards linked to UPI or pre-sanctioned bank credit lines, operate under separate credit product rules.
As a result, the MDR won’t apply to these transactions in the same manner as direct bank-account-to-merchant UPI payments.
How Will The MDR Revenue Be Divided?
The 0.4% MDR paid by the merchant will flow through different parts of the UPI ecosystem. In effect, the ₹0.40 MDR is split as 0.28% for the issuer bank, 0.08% for the TPAP and 0.04% for the acquiring bank.
For every ₹100 eligible UPI transaction, the merchant will pay ₹0.40 as MDR to the acquiring bank, which is the bank handling the merchant’s UPI account.
Of this ₹0.40, ₹0.28 (0.28%) will be paid by the acquiring bank to the customer’s issuing bank as interchange. A further ₹0.08 (0.08%) will go to the UPI app provider, paid by the payer-side payment service provider (PSP). This leaves ₹0.04 (0.04%) with the acquiring bank.
Why Is UPI Introducing MDR Now?
The move comes as UPI has scaled to become one of India’s primary digital payment systems.
UPI processed 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026 alone.
The policy framework argues that operating a payment system at this scale requires significant spending on server infrastructure, bandwidth, fraud prevention, cybersecurity and banking technology.
Industry estimates cited in the framework put the annual cost of maintaining UPI operations at around ₹20,000 Cr.
Until now, government incentives and subsidies have helped support the ecosystem. The new framework argues that these were intended as short-term support rather than a permanent mechanism for covering payment infrastructure costs.
The MDR revenue will be retained within the UPI ecosystem and is intended to support infrastructure resilience, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service. It will also
What Happens To The MDR Money?
A dedicated fund for small merchants is also proposed under the framework.
The fund will be used to support digital payment infrastructure in Tier III to Tier IV centres, including the northeastern states, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. It will also cover notified government schemes in Tier I and Tier II centres.
The fund is expected to provide financial assistance to acquiring banks and payment aggregators for merchant onboarding and incentivise UPI transactions among small merchants.
The detailed framework for the fund is expected to be finalised in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India within three months.
Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly intensified its scrutiny of big tech giant Apple’s software warranty terms.
This is part of the watchdog’s broader investigation into issues linked to the smartphone maker’s iOS 18 update, which allegedly damaged iPhone functionality and compelled users to pay “exorbitant” sums for repairs.
As per documents accessed by Reuters, the CCPA, in June, ​told Apple that it had “escalated” the matter for a “detailed investigation” by its investigation wing. The iPhone is said to have responded to the regulator’s investigation.
In a statement sent to Inc42, the company said that it primarily sells hardware, adding that software is something that goes along with the device. The company added that no tech company, including Apple, across the globe offers warranty on software
Apple also said that it closely monitors user feedback after every software update, and that it did not identify any issues, safety concerns, or similar trends related to the launch of iOS 18 in India. The iPhone maker also noted that it is open to working with local authorities to provide clarity on the customer response to iOS 18.
The development comes over a year after the CCPA issued a notice to Apple. This came after the watchdog received multiple complaints regarding performance issues of iPhones following the iOS 18+ software update.
Notably, this is not the first time that the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) has come under the radar of Indian authorities. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has already found Apple guilty of abusing its dominant position in the app store market.
The big tech giant is already contesting the matter and has accused the CCI of “copy-pasting” allegations made by rival companies instead of conducting an independent probe into its App Store practices.
Even as it grapples with issues related to the iOS18 software update, Apple began rolling out iOS 27 yesterday, which comes with Siri AI. However, critics have flagged that the new AI features are only available for its premium, higher-end devices, creating a two-tier model for its iPhone users.
Despite this, Apple continues to double down on India. Earlier this month, the big tech giant launched its first foldable smartphone, called iPhone Duo, which will be available in India at a starting price of ₹3 Lakh for a 256 GB model. It also unveiled its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models.
The launches came as Apple clocked record revenue in June 2026 quarter in India. At the time, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh also said India delivered strong double-digit revenue growth during the quarter, with Mac emerging as one of the standout performers.
Besides sales, India continues to be a major manufacturing hub for Apple. Over the years, the company has significantly expanded local iPhone production, with iPhone exports from India crossing the ₹2 Lakh Cr mark in FY26.
The post CCPA Orders Detailed Probe Into Apple Over iOS 18 Software Issues appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
India’s AI story is moving beyond models, and the next quest is about how AI is being deployed, integrated into workflows, governed and navigated to deliver measurable value.
Last month, Inc42 reported that enterprise LLM adoption in India is taking a vertical turn, with companies such as Razorpay, Fractal, BharatGen and Tech Mahindra building models for payments, healthcare, agriculture and education rather than general-purpose chat.
A fortnight ago, we reported that enterprise AI deployment was getting a reality check, with organisations imposing budget caps, approval gates and unit-economics scrutiny on AI features well before they reach production.
This suggests that value is shifting towards the layer where AI is deployed, governed and measured, and away from the layer where it is merely demonstrated.
The ecosystem data agrees. The Bharat AI Startups Report 2026, published by Inc42 with Google, put India’s AI market at $126 Bn by 2030, led by enterprise AI growing from $11 Bn to $71 Bn, and noted that 47% of enterprises are already moving pilots into production.
Capital is following the same logic. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, nearly four times the $162 Mn raised in the same period last year, according to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, even as overall startup funding slipped 9%.
But the more telling signal is not how much capital is flowing into AI. It is which problems capital is being asked to solve.
Against this backdrop, Inc42 returns with its monthly AI Startups To Watch series. The twelfth edition highlights five emerging startups building across AI operations, education, sovereign compute, financial services deployment and enterprise execution.
These are not simply startups using AI as a feature. They are trying to build businesses at the point where AI stops being a demo and starts carrying consequences.
With that said, here are the five emerging AI startups that caught our attention in September.
Editor’s Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically.
Oppex AI | Helping Engineers Detect, Investigate, Resolve Production Incidents Faster
Every time a company ships new code, something can break in production. Engineers get paged, often at night, then lose hours finding what went wrong. Clues sit scattered across logs, dashboards, customer complaints, and old fix notes, and alerts pile up faster than a small team can clear them.
Oppex AI is trying to automate that work. Founded in 2025 by Prasun Kumar and Pranit Kumar, the Bengaluru startup has built an AI system that reads across a company’s monitoring tools, support tickets, cloud systems and internal notes, then points to the likely bug.
The platform groups alerts describing the same issue into one incident, learns a company’s setup so its answers improve over time, and remembers earlier fixes so nothing is lost when the on-duty engineer changes.
Oppex says its agents resolve issues five times faster with half the on-call engineers. Within eight months of writing its first line of code, it deployed its platform across enterprises in India, the UK, the EU, and the US, targeting the global AIOps market, projected to reach $41.6 Bn by 2030 at a 30.3% CAGR.
ProLearn | AI-Native Learning Companion
Personal tutoring works. It has simply never scaled. Most Indian students preparing for board exams or entrance tests still learn from recorded lectures and static test papers, with little feedback on where exactly their understanding breaks down.
ProLearn is trying to put that attention inside a phone. The Bengaluru startup was founded in April 2026 by Ravneet Singh, a former Vedantu executive. He is building an AI-native learning companion for K-12 students and aspirants preparing for JEE, NEET, UPSC and CAT.
The companion is built for conversation rather than content delivery. It listens to how a student explains a problem, asks questions back, adapts to their pace and walks them through a solution step by step, the way a tutor would.
ProLearn raised ₹30 Cr in a pre-seed round led by BEENEXT to build its AI and reasoning infrastructure and curriculum-aligned content ahead of a public launch. It is targeting India’s AI tutors market projected to reach $1.2 Bn by 2031.
Quantum Tiger | Sovereign AI Systems For Architectural Autonomy
Most enterprises running serious AI workloads still do it on someone else’s infrastructure, sending sensitive data across borders to models and cloud services they do not control. For banks, hospitals, defence contractors and government institutions, that is becoming unacceptable, commercially and legally.
Quantum Tiger wants to make the alternative smaller. The Kolkata-based startup was founded in 2025 by Rana Dutta and Manas Paul, and is building full-stack sovereign AI infrastructure that lets organisations train and run AI workloads within their own trusted boundaries, without depending on public cloud infrastructure.
Its stack pairs an AI operating layer with purpose-built compute hardware designed to run large language models locally at predictable latency, doing training and inference on the same system so enterprises are not billed for every external call. The company says the system is engineered for data locality and continuous model adaptation across heterogeneous workloads.
Quantum Tiger is targeting the sovereign AI infrastructure market, estimated at $15 Bn in 2025 and projected to reach $177.09 Bn by 2035.
Vecton AI | Production-Ready AI For BFSI
Financial services is where AI promises the most and delivers the least. Banks and insurers sit on decades of structured data and repetitive, high-volume processes, yet most AI pilots inside them never leave the sandbox, held back by regulatory requirements, legacy architecture and the cost of reworking core systems.
Vecton AI is built to solve just that. Founded in 2025 by Himanshu Goyal and Gaurav Mandlecha, the Bengaluru startup positions itself as an AI transformation partner for banks, financial services and insurance companies.
It works across AI consulting and strategy, process automation, custom-trained models and autonomous agent development, with a delivery model built on forward-deployed engineers who stay with the client through implementation.
It ships production-ready, compliant agent systems and machine learning workflows aligned with BFSI regulatory standards, focussed on sales acceleration, customer engagement, document processing, and intelligent copilots.
Vecton is targeting India’s AI in BFSI market, estimated at $1,069 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $9,425.2 Mn by 2034.
Zenalyst | AI Workforce For Enterprises
Every CIO says the same thing: dashboards everywhere, answers nowhere. Enterprise decisions still depend on numbers scattered across ERP, CRM, banking and document systems, stitched together by hand. By the time a finance team spots a variance, the quarter it belonged to is closed.
Zenalyst is building agents that do the work rather than describe it. The Bengaluru-based startup was founded in May 2025 by Nagendra Singh, Sanketh Krishnappa and Vijay Jha, and its ZenForce platform connects to more than 150 enterprise systems across ERP, CRM and banking to run finance, procurement and legal workflows. Zenalyst is targeting the autonomous finance market, projected to reach $112.84 Bn by 2031.
Its agents include ZenBank for treasury and money operations, ZenProcure for procurement and ZenCollect for order-to-cash and contract intelligence. Zenalyst positions ZenForce as deterministic rather than probabilistic: reasoning is gated through verification steps, queries are grounded in the customer’s own schema, and customer data is never used to train external models.
With inputs from Venu Rathore
Edited by Shishir Parasher
Creatives by Abhyam Gusai
The post AI Startups To Watch: 5 Startups That Caught Our Eye In September appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: NITDA
items.content:
By Naeemah Junaid
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON) have renewed their commitment to deploying digital technology to enhance Hajj administration, improve operational efficiency and strengthen service delivery to Nigerian pilgrims.
The commitment was reached when the Chairman of NAHCON, Ambassador Ismail Abba Yusuf, led a delegation of the Commission on a strategic visit to NITDA headquarters in Abuja, where he met with the Director-General of the Agency, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, CCIE.
The engagement focused on strengthening technical cooperation between the two institutions and exploring practical ways of integrating technology across the various stages of Hajj operations.
Speaking during the meeting, Inuwa said NITDA was ready to support NAHCON in building a more coordinated and sustainable digital framework for Hajj administration.
He noted that the complexity of Hajj operations, which involves registration, payments, aviation, accommodation, transportation, feeding, healthcare and the movement of large numbers of pilgrims, required systems capable of working together seamlessly.
The NITDA DG cautioned against treating digital transformation as a one-time technology project, stressing that sustainable transformation required continuous improvement and institutional commitment.
“Digital transformation is not a one-off project. It is a journey and a journey that needs constant improvement,” he said.
Inuwa explained that technology should be deployed as an enabler of institutional objectives and not as an end in itself.
“Digital transformation is not just about technology. It is about your business value proposition. It is about the business, not technology. Technology enables you to deliver your business objectives,” he added.
He urged NAHCON to address the challenge of siloed systems by developing an integrated digital architecture that would allow information to move efficiently across different aspects of Hajj administration.
According to him, an integrated system would provide end-to-end visibility of operations, improve coordination and enable management to make timely, data-driven decisions.
The NITDA DG also drew attention to the growing relevance of artificial intelligence and intelligent digital systems, noting that emerging technologies could provide new opportunities for improving institutional processes and service delivery.
He recalled NITDA’s previous support to NAHCON in areas including training and process documentation, expressing the Agency’s readiness to build on the existing relationship through renewed technical collaboration.
Inuwa further encouraged the Commission to explore Public-Private Partnership (PPP) models in implementing major digital projects, noting that such arrangements could attract private-sector expertise and investment while reducing the financial burden on government.
He said NITDA would also continue to promote quality and value for money in government technology projects through proper system design, certified implementation and independent quality assurance.
On capacity development, the DG assured NAHCON of the Agency’s readiness to support training for ICT personnel and digital orientation for state coordinators and other stakeholders involved in Hajj administration.
He stressed that successful digital transformation must become embedded in the institution and should not depend on the tenure of individual officials.
“It is not about the board. It is not about just the chairman. It is about the institution,” Inuwa said.
Earlier, the NAHCON Chairman, Ambassador IsmailIsmail A. Yusuf, said the Commission’s visit was prompted by the need to accelerate the digitalisation of Hajj arrangements in Nigeria and align its operations with global best practices.
Yusuf noted that Saudi Arabia had made significant advances in the digital management of Hajj, adding that Nigeria needed to strengthen its systems to improve coordination and service delivery.
While acknowledging the progress already recorded by NAHCON, he said several processes remained manual and required further automation and integration.
“We’re trying to digitise Hajj arrangements in line with global best practice,” the Chairman said.
He explained that NAHCON was seeking NITDA’s technical expertise in areas such as system assessment, capacity building, process improvement, data management and the integration of existing digital platforms.
The Chairman said closer cooperation with NITDA would help strengthen the Commission’s digital infrastructure and ensure better coordination of information between Nigerian and Saudi systems.
“That is why our cooperation with NITDA is very, very important, that we work together. We are on the same page in everything we do. We compare notes and all that,” he said.
Presenting an overview of NAHCON’s digital solutions, the Commission’s Head of ICT, Shehu Raji said several platforms had been developed in-house despite budgetary constraints.
These include electronic registration, package and programme management, aviation management, automated flight manifests, seating distribution, real-time logistics, accommodation allocation, feeding management, electronic medical records, passport release management and the Hajj Companion application.
He said the Hajj Companion application provides pilgrims with mapped information on accommodation and major Hajj locations in Makkah, Madinah, Mina and Arafat, helping them navigate the various sites during the pilgrimage.
However, Raji noted that some of the systems were only partially deployed and required further development, integration and technical support.
He said improved interoperability would eliminate unnecessary duplication of data entry, enhance data accuracy and facilitate better coordination of pilgrim information.
Raji also emphasised the importance of data security and integrity, noting that reliable information was critical to effective accommodation, transportation, security and other Hajj arrangements.
At the conclusion of the engagement, both institutions agreed to strengthen their partnership through technical collaboration, capacity building, system integration, process improvement and quality assurance.
The two organisations also agreed on the proposed establishment of a technical working group to coordinate priority areas and ensure sustained engagement.
The renewed partnership is expected to advance the development of a more integrated, secure and efficient digital Hajj ecosystem in Nigeria, while improving accountability, reducing manual processes and enhancing the overall experience of Nigerian pilgrims.

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on ride unicorn Rapido for misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, unfair contract and dark patterns, where consumers are prompted to pay more before their rides are confirmed.
The order, passed by a bench comprising chief commissioner Nidhi Khare and commissioner Anupam Mishra, follows a sector-wide examination of cab aggregators operating in India to understand pre-ride tipping and dynamic pricing practices in India.
During the investigation, the CCPA found that Rapido’s app displayed users prompts suggesting specific top-ups of ₹10, ₹20 or ₹30 to improve their chances of getting a ride.
The regulator held that Rapido’s algorithm first quoted a fare, and then, once the rider had booked at that fare, asked the rider to pay more because ‘Captains’ (drivers) were supposedly not accepting the fare. That created a false impression that getting a ride quickly depends on paying extra fees.
The CCPA held this to be “confirm shaming”, a dark pattern listed under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, as it creates urgency and a fear of losing the ride if the rider does not agree to pay more.
Separately, the regulator examined Rapido’s “set your price” slider and found its colour coding was steering pricing decisions. Raising the price surfaced a green message about a higher chance of getting a ride, while lowering it triggered a red or orange warning.
This design, the CCPA held, amounted to a second dark pattern — “interface interference”.
A tip, as the regulator observed, is a voluntary payment made after a service has been rendered, and can not be presented as a condition for the service being provided at all.
It also pointed to the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, which require any tipping feature to be offered only after a ride is completed — not at the time of booking or during the ride.
Rapido had argued that tipping on its platform is voluntary, and that the prompts simply mirrored the kind of real-time negotiation that happens offline between a rider and a driver.
The CCPA rejected these submissions, holding that the timing and design of the prompts applied pressure at the moment the users seemed to be the most dependent on the platform. It also noted that Rapido had not shown any data to show that paying more actually improves a rider’s chances of getting a ride, making the claim unsubstantiated and misleading.
The action against Rapido is part of the CCPA’s broader scrutiny of advance-tip and dark-pattern practices across ride-hailing and bike-taxi platforms.
The regulator had earlier issued notices to Uber, Ola, Rapido and Namma Yatri, directing them to comply with the 2023 dark patterns guidelines and file self-declarations on compliance. Its examination of Uber and Ola is still ongoing.
Besides, it also adds to the ongoing regulatory scrutiny over the advance tipping dark patterns employed by ride-hailing platforms. Earlier in August, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) directed ride-hailing aggregators to remove tipping prompts shown before or during rides, saying these violate the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025.
The ministry reiterated that passengers can tip drivers only after completing a ride, with the entire amount going to the driver. Platforms also cannot suggest that tipping could improve ride confirmation, driver acceptance or service quality.
The directive comes amid wider scrutiny of aggregators, including NHRC action over alleged overcharging. The 2025 guidelines also cover licensing, driver training and insurance, vehicle safety, fares and penalties, including licences of up to five years and fines of up to ₹1 Cr.
