items.author: Meha Agarwal
items.content:
Kids want a bar of chocolate, but parents want a healthier snacking option. For years, this has been one of the toughest equations for nutrition-conscious parents, who often found themselves negotiating tantrums in the kids’ food aisle of every supermarket.
A new crop of Indian D2C brands believes it has found a way around that tug-of-war. Their proposition is simple: don’t ask children to eat differently but make the food they already love better.
One example is Little Joys. It is betting that adding protein to a ‘roti’ is easier than getting a child to try a new food. The health and wellness platform launched a protein mix to add into the dough and batter for rotis, dosas and pancakes.
That’s one example of how healthy snacking and kids-centric food is getting a revamp. Jaipur-based Gladful puts sprouted lentils and millets into familiar breakfast mixes, while The Whole Truth’s Next Gen range includes milk mixes, snack bars and protein blocks.
For the urban millennial parents these brands are targeting, paying a premium can be easier than finding the time to prepare everything from scratch. But the purchase still has to satisfy two people: the child who eats the product and the parent who pays for it.
Little Joys’ founder Revant Bhate told us, “The hard thing in building a kids brand is building for two customers. A 10-year-old wants great taste, while a parent wants proof that the product is good and effective. And the bar for winning both over keeps getting higher.”
Meanwhile, parents aren’t the only ones scrutinising what these brands are promising. In June, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) flagged 15 brands, including Storia, Two Brothers Organic Farms, PLAN B, The Health Factory, Troovy and Emami’s Healthy & Tasty, over allegedly misleading branding and claims. Expressions such as “healthy”, “organic”, “zero maida” and “vegan” came under scrutiny.
This leaves us with a question: can these brands convince parents that better ingredients and better formulations are worth paying for?
The Fine Print Behind ‘Healthy’
The market is crowded with both legacy and new-age brands offering products positioned as healthier options for children. But what are these brands bringing to the table?
According to Gladful cofounder Parul Sharma, brands are trying to balance nutrition, taste and trust with information on actual formulation, laboratory analysis and compliance with FSSAI requirements. Serving sizes and nutritional values should also be relevant to the age group being addressed.
She also pointed to the ICMR’s recommended dietary allowances for children aged seven to nine. The ICMR’s nutrient requirements framework distinguishes between average requirements, recommended allowances and upper limits.
Sharma also said finding the right balance is a challenge for many brands. For instance, reducing sugar or changing conventional ingredients can affect taste and texture. Similarly, using higher-quality or more recognisable ingredients can increase formulation and ingredient costs.
Talking about clean labels, Mansi Baranwal, the cofounder of Troovy cofounder, said most brands highlight healthier ingredients such as pulses, millets and jaggery on their labels, but often list “spices and condiments” at the end.
“These spices and condiments may contain silicon dioxide, disodium inosinate, disodium guanylate and tertiary butylhydroquinone, or TBHQ, alongside artificial colours and flavours, emulsifiers, firming agents and gelling agents. My concern is how far brands are willing to go in reworking these parts of the recipe to keep their ingredient promises,” she added.
Baranwal said leaving out these ingredients means the seasoning would not stick evenly, leading to repeated failed batches and lakhs spent on innovation. Troovy now spends approximately ₹10-12 Lakh a month on laboratory testing, covering raw materials and finished products.
Baranwal’s concern is that brands should not stop at asking whether an additive is allowed today. They should also keep looking at the evidence behind its use. At the same time, an unfamiliar ingredient name does not automatically mean it is unsafe.
Surviving The Cost Sheet
A young brand needs suppliers willing to work with small orders, unfamiliar formulations, and repeated trials. Baranwal of Troovy said that combination can make manufacturers reluctant. The volumes may not justify the effort, and the innovation adds risk.
This also leaves founders doing work that a larger food company can spread across specialist teams. “In a startup a small team is managing everything -R&D, procurement, production, quality, manufacturer relationships. And they also have to handle testing and compliance with the same level of diligence as the giants,” she added.
Then comes the next- ingredient bill. Prices of better oils, protein ingredients, alternate sweeteners, and nuts are high. And have risen further in recent months. Most brands, so far, have absorbed some of that increase through lower gross margins rather than passing the entire cost on to consumers.
So where can the savings come from?
Sharma pointed to procurement, manufacturing scale, packaging, production yields and distribution. She argues that brands need to make the entire operation more efficient instead of simply cutting ingredients.
Shelf life is another part of the equation. It has to work not just at the manufacturing stage, but through distribution and the time a product spends in a household.
Sunitha Vishwanathan, partner at Kae Capital, believes brands concentrating only on D2C and quick commerce risk building on too narrow a base. Established food companies already have the retail reach that challengers are trying to build, and moving into those stores requires rethinking what each pack earns.
“The pack sizes, price points, and margin structures that work on Blinkit don’t automatically translate to a kirana shelf or a supermarket aisle.”
That means a recipe that works in production still needs a pack size and selling price that works wherever the parent buys it. Otherwise, wider distribution can bring more orders without resolving the margin problem.
Winning A Place In The Next Grocery Basket
Farmley’s 2026 snacking survey, which covered more than 6,000 respondents across cities and age groups, found that nearly 60% of the parents surveyed were willing to pay a premium for healthier snacks for their children. This is an encouraging signal, but willingness to pay is only the first step.
Vishwanathan believes that with so many brands claiming to offer healthier snacks, the real edge will come from specific, demonstrable nutritional benefits rather than another list of ingredients that a product does not contain.
She pointed to areas such as protein for active children, gut health and cognitive support as propositions companies are exploring. But these are still claims that need evidence.
For Sharma, the clearest commercial evidence comes from watching what households do after the trial. Are they buying again? How long does the next order take? Does the product still sell once the introductory offer ends? She also looks at revenue from returning customers, retention over time and whether families use the products across everyday eating occasions.
“Ultimately, the strongest signal is whether consumers stop thinking of the product as something they “try because it is healthier” and start buying it because it has become part of their regular household food routine,” Sharma added.
For now, these brands have found parents willing to listen. As they grow, the harder decisions will come when an ingredient gets costlier, or a retailer asks for a bigger margin. What they choose to protect then will tell us how much their promise is worth.
SPOTLIGHT| Inside Poco Mico’s Premium Kidswear Play
Founded in 2024, Poco Mico is a kidswear D2C brand that offers premium and durable clothing for children, alongside home care products such as crib mattresses, cushion covers and mats. It is designed for children up to 10 years old.
The brand caters to different age groups and occasions, with its portfolio spanning casual wear, party wear and wedding wear for children. Its D2C-first model allows it to target parents looking for premium everyday and occasion-led kidswear.
Poco Mico claims to use certified cotton with its soft-skin-touch technology, designed to provide comfort while retaining the fabric’s size and colour and reducing shrinkage. The brand only sells products via its own website.
The Deep Dive
Ecommerce Buzz
AppsForBharat Data Dispute: A Bengaluru court has restrained Veda Mandir parent Way2News from using AppsForBharat’s confidential data and IP after allegations of proprietary data sharing by a former employee. AppsForBharat is seeking ₹1 Cr in damages.
Zomato’s COD Tantrum: The foodtech giant has started levying a separate fee on some cash-on-delivery orders, ranging from ₹5 to ₹13, with some users reporting charges as high as ₹21. The payment-linked fee comes as Zomato looks to boost monetisation and encourage online payments.
Triptii Dimri’s Beauty Bet: The actor has joined eye-focused D2C beauty startup Peep Beauty as an investor and co-creator. Founded by former Keventers cofounder Aman Arora, the startup has raised ₹12 Cr and is building around coloured contact lenses and eye makeup.
The Operator Question
What are the biggest challenges in building a kids’ nutrition brand for children aged 6-14 in India, and what does it take to get the product, parental trust and repeat purchases right at an early stage?
We reached out to Astha Jain, the cofounder of kids’ ayurvedic wellness brand Ayuvya, to understand the playbook here. Here’s what she divulged:
Tailored Customer Experience: A new buyer and a returning one have completely different questions. New customers need education around how to use the product, what to expect and when they can realistically see results, while returning customers need continuity through dosage reminders and the next steps in their regimen. In Ayurveda, where results depend on consistent use over weeks, getting the first-timer journey right is critical to driving the second order.
Use Check-Ins To Prevent Silent Churn: Instead of reaching out only when it is time to sell again, Ayuvya uses structured check-ins after purchase. Day 7 helps identify usage mistakes before customers give up, while Day 14 checks for early signs of progress. This allows the brand to address issues during the usage journey and makes the eventual reorder part of an ongoing conversation rather than a cold sales pitch.
Rope In Doctors To Build Trust And Improve Outcomes: Ayuvya offers free consultations with its Ayurvedic doctors to help customers choose and use the right products. Jain believes personalised guidance improves adherence and outcomes while addressing a larger trust problem in the category, where customers have often encountered exaggerated or fake Ayurvedic claims. A conversation with a practitioner can build more trust than marketing communication alone, she added.
The post Kids’ Nutrition Brands Face A Familiar Struggle appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.content:
Apple’s High-Stakes Gamble On Siri AI
Two years on, Apple’s rebuilt Siri AI has now finally arrived with iOS 27. But most of its advanced AI features are limited to premium devices, feature access remains uneven and a subscription model may be on the horizon. So, will Siri AI justify the price?
The Long-Awaited Siri: The new launch is Apple’s attempt to turn its voice assistant into a more personal, context-aware interface. Siri AI can draw on information across messages, email and photos, understand what is on screen and act within compatible apps. But not everyone will get to experience the full version.
A Fragmented Experience? The iOS 27 update will reach a broad group of iPhones, but Apple Intelligence and Siri AI will require newer devices. Advanced features will need higher memory and have been reserved for select premium products. This creates a two-tier experience: many users can access Siri AI, but only high-end devices will be able to receive its fullest version.
The India Test: Just like its US peers, Indian users will also receive broad availability for several Apple Intelligence tools. But availability does not guarantee a seamless experience. Siri AI must understand local accents, different speech patterns and multilingual habits if it is to feel truly useful in India. Early reports suggest uneven reliability in routine tasks even though users expect an assistant to be fast and dependable.
The New Apple Tax: The cost question extends beyond buying an AI-ready iPhone. Apple has indicated that some server-based AI features will have usage caps, adding that higher access could carry a fee from 2027 onward. This could push Siri AI into a tiered subscription model, likely linked to iCloud+. On top of this, developers will also have to quickly build compatible apps for Siri AI.
So, can Apple turn Siri AI into a must-have service rather than another expensive ecosystem lock-in? Let’s find out…
From The Editor’s Desk
Moneyview Trims IPO Size
The fintech unicorn has halved the size of its fresh issue to ₹750 Cr as against ₹1,500 Cr proposed earlier. It has also slashed its offer for sale component to 10.04 Cr equity shares from 13.6 Cr previously.
This comes as early backers such as Tiger Global, Accel, Crimson Winter, Ribbit Capital and others have cut the number of shares they intend to offload. However, Moneyview did not disclose the timeline for the opening of its public issue.
Founded in 2014, Moneyview runs a digital-first lending platform that provides unsecured personal loans to underserved and new-to-credit customers. It has raised over $250 Mn to date and had AUM worth ₹19,814 Cr at the end of December 2025.
Rumblings At InsuranceDekho
The IPO-bound startup’s cofounders – CEO Ankit Agrawal and CTO Ish Babbar – are looking to step down from their executive roles due to disagreement with board members about the strategic direction of the recently merged business.
With a potential IPO on the horizon, the startup’s two founders could likely move into promoter roles while professional management takes over the business. However, the startup has denied that the cofounders are looking to exit from their executive roles.
This comes days after InsuranceDekho announced the completion of its merger with rival insurance distributor RenewBuy. The combined entity claims that its premium book is worth over ₹6,600 Cr and it offers more than 750 insurance products.
Lenskart Doubles Down On AjnaLens
The omnichannel eyewear giant has acquired an additional 1.8% stake in the extended reality startup’s parent Dimension NXG for ₹8 Cr. With this, Lenskart’s holding in AjnaLens has increased to 9.01% from 7.21% earlier.
Lenskart first invested in the startup in July last year. It then picked up an additional 0.68% stake in February this year and another 1.69% shareholding in July. Together, these three deals cost the listed company ₹18.5 Cr.
The deals come as Lenskart looks to strengthen its foothold in the XR, AI and smart wearable technology ecosystems. It has already debuted its Phonic audio glasses and plans to launch AI-powered smart glasses soon.
RBI’s New Cyber Safety Protocols
The Reserve Bank of India has proposed a new framework, which establishes a uniform procedure for banks dealing with accounts and transactions suspected of being linked to money-mule activity or cyber-enabled financial fraud.
The proposed framework directs banks to freeze only the suspected transaction amount rather than the entire account. A temporary debit-hold will only be permitted as a last resort when the account itself is suspected to be a money-mule account.
Account holders would get 20 days to explain the account activity, after which the bank must review the response within 10 days. The draft rules are scheduled to take effect from April 1, 2027.
Google’s New Accelerator Cohort
The big tech giant has selected four Indian startups for the maiden cohort of its ‘AI for the Planet (APAC)’ accelerator initiative, which aims to address urgent environmental challenges using AI.
The four startups — Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon — will join a cohort of 16 startups operating across the Asia Pacific region.
Over the next three months, these startups will receive access to the Google AI stack, tailored technical support and expert mentorship to scale their sustainability-focused AI solutions.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How Saubha Aerial Systems Is Putting Parachutes On Drones
From logistics to defence, drones are moving into new sectors every day. Yet, one motor failure can turn a valuable aircraft into a falling object. Saubha Aerial Systems is building the safety layer to make unmanned aerial vehicles more reliable and resilient.
Safety Net For Drones: Founded in 2025, Saubha is building aerospace-grade safety and security systems for unmanned aircraft. The startup’s product portfolio includes emergency recovery systems for drones, including parachutes, ejection mechanisms and trigger systems. Its Para range supports payloads from 4 kg to 25 kg and is designed to bring drones down at roughly 5 m/s, reducing damage to both the aircraft and people or property below.
Saubha’s Product Stack: The Bengaluru-based startup has developed three parachute deployment mechanisms. Springshot uses a spring-powered system for smaller drones, Airlaunch relies on compressed air for rapid deployment and Pyrolaunch uses a pyrotechnic mechanism for mission-critical applications.
The Emergency Trigger: The startup’s Mayday Autonomous Flight Trigger monitors flight behaviour through multiple sensors and can activate the recovery system when it detects a critical failure. Meanwhile, Lifeline provides a manual, pilot-controlled alternative. It also offers customised recovery systems based on payload and other operating conditions.
As drones become more common, can Saubha make emergency recovery systems a standard safety feature in Indian UAVs?
Infographic Of The Day
From Emergent to SatSure, homegrown ventures are building the models, infrastructure and products shaping the country’s AI boom. So, which top tech executives are building the tech behind India’s biggest AI bets?

Reserve Bank of India announces the auction of Government of India Treasury Bills as per the following details:
Sr. No. Treasury Bill Notified Amount
(₹ crore) Auction Date Settlement Date
1 91-Day 9,000 September 16, 2026
(Wednesday) September 17, 2026
(Thursday)
2 182-Day 8,000
3 364-Day 7,000
  Total 24,000    
The sale will be subject to the terms and conditions specified in the General Notification F.No.4(2)-B(W&M)/2018 dated March 26, 2025, issued by Government of India, as amended from time to time. State Governments, Union Territories with legislature, eligible Provident Funds in India, designated Foreign Central Banks and any person or institution specified by the Bank in this regard can participate on non-competitive basis, the allocation for which will be outside the notified amount. Individuals can also participate on non-competitive basis, as retail investors. For retail investors, the allocation will be restricted to a maximum of 5 percent of the notified amount. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
The auction will be Price based using multiple price method. Bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India’s Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber system) on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, during the below given timings:
Category of Bids Timing
Competitive 10:30 am - 11:30 am
Non-Competitive 10:30 am - 11:00 am
Results will be announced on the day of the auction.
Payment by successful bidders will have to be made on Thursday, September 17, 2026.
Only in the event of system failure, physical bids would be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190), before the auction timing ends, in the prescribed form. The form can be downloaded from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx). In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted at email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125).
Ajit Prasad          
Deputy General Manager
(Communications)

items.content:
By Benjamin Njoku
The Federal Ministry of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy has reaffirmed its commitment to partner with state governments, investors, creative entrepreneurs, technology platforms, hospitality businesses and other stakeholders to build an ecosystem that can unlock Nigeria’s $100 billion tourism and creative economy potential.
Speaking at the official flag-off of “Ember to Remember 2026” and the unveiling of the national calendar in Lagos on Monday, Minister Hannatu Musa Musawa said the ministry is working toward a tourism and creative economy that contributes meaningfully to Nigeria’s GDP all year round.
According to her, the goal is an economy that creates opportunities for young Nigerians, attracts investment, strengthens local businesses, and projects Nigeria positively to the world.
“Ember to Remember 2026” is a 100-day national tourism season running from September to December.
Musawa said it aligns with President Bola Tinubu’s economic vision to expand Nigeria’s economic base, unlock new growth sectors, create jobs, and position the private sector as a key driver of national development.
“Our ambition must, however, go beyond December. It requires deliberate planning, collaboration, investment and execution to drive this initiative,” she said.
“The $100 billion opportunity will not be created by one ministry, one company or one event. It will be created by an ecosystem. And that ecosystem is represented in this room today. So I challenge every organisation here to ask: What role can we play in building Nigeria’s next major economic growth sector?
“Let this conference mark the beginning of a stronger partnership between government and the private sector. Let us make Ember to Remember a platform that connects our destinations, our events, our businesses and our people to a much larger national and global market
“And most importantly, let us populate the calendar, promote Nigeria and convert our celebrations into sustainable economic value. Nigeria has the culture. Nigeria has the creativity. Nigeria has the people. Nigeria has the market. Now, we must build the economy around it,”_ Musawa said.
The Minister tasked the private sector to lead the transformation, while government provides the enabling environment through policy, infrastructure, security, destination development and ease of movement.
She also commended Mrs. Ifeoma Chukwu, CEO of MyCityApp, for her commitment, assuring all partners of the ministry’s support.
“This is precisely the kind of partnership we must encourage, where government provides the enabling environment while innovative Nigerians create platforms, products and opportunities that move our economy forward. This initiative is about moving beyond the traditional concept of a festive season. It is about deliberately organising, packaging, promoting and monetising one of the most economically active periods in our national calendar,” she added.
Also speaking, Ifeoma Chukwu said the essence of the initiative is to promote Nigeria’s cultural, tourism and creative offerings from September to December.
The calendar is expected to help Nigerians, members of the diaspora and international visitors discover events and experiences across Nigeria’s 36 states and the FCT.
“MyCityApp is a digital city and tourism platform connecting people to Nigeria’s events, destinations, hospitality, culture and experiences. Nigeria is rich in culture with one of the most vibrant creative industries in the world. The opportunity is to turn every visitor’s experience into economic value. That is how celebration becomes commerce. And tourism becomes an economy,” Chukwu said.
In attendance were Mr. Babajide Olusola Sanwo Olu, Executive Governor of Lagos State, who was represented by Honorable Toke Benson-Awoyink, the Lagos State Commissioner for Tourism, Arts and Culture, His excellency Dr, Peter Ndubisi Mbah, Governor of Enugu State,also represented by Honorable Barrister Ugochi Madueke, the Enugu State Commissioner for Culture and Tourism,
His excellency Alhaji Mohammed Idris Malagi, the Honorable Minister of Information and National Orientation of Nigeria, represented by Dr. Olalekan Fadolapo, Director General of the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) among other stakeholders.
The post FG targets $100bn tourism, creative economy with ‘Ember To Remember 2026’ national season appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
Technicians Holding Fort -HMB
By Egufe Yafugborhi
ASABA – Health services in public hospitals across Delta State have come under pressure as the ongoing strike by allied health professionals escalated, with affected workers insisting they will not return to work until their demands are addressed.
The Nigerian Union of Allied Health Professionals, NUAHP, said the strike followed months of unsuccessful engagements with the state government over allowances and other conditions affecting its members.
State Chairman of NUAHP, Comrade Uruwayino Charles Samuel Jr, narrated to Vanguard on Monday that, “On February 1st, we started engaging the Ministry of Health on three issues.
“Initially, it was three issues: the payment of 16 months arrears of the peculiar allowance, which was implemented in 2024, and the implementation of the circular on the review of allowances of health practitioners.
“We wrote to the Ministry of Health, Asaba, to engage them to implement that circular because these two demands have been paid to doctors in state employment. We submitted those circulars in February.”
He said the union’s demands were expanded after the state government approved a N200,000 monthly preferential allowance for medical doctors.
“So immediately, we declared a three-day warning strike in April. The commissioner (for health, Dr. Joseph Onojaemo) invited us and other stakeholders to a meeting.
“At that meeting, through his spokesman, he stated that the NLC and TUC had concluded that affiliates should forego the peculiar allowance because it was forgone for the implementation of the minimum wage.
“Nothing was said about the preferential allowance. When we raised our hands to ask questions, the Commissioner ended the meeting.”
Uruwayino said subsequent engagements led to the constitution of a committee in August to determine the financial implications of the workers’ demands.
“The committee agreed with us. For the preferential allowance, the committee agreed to N180,000. For the peculiar allowance, the committee agreed to 16 months of arrears.
“Everything was compiled, and the report was presented to the Honourable Commissioner, who accepted it without raising any argument, meaning there was a resolution to the dispute.”
He alleged that the implementation of the committee’s recommendations was subsequently delayed.
“When it came to paying us, he (Commissioner) started singing a different tune after all our efforts since February. He asked us to give him four months, then two months,” he said.
Uruwayino added: “The commissioner has now given us a formal invite, and hopefully we will meet this week on Thursday. But we are still going to continue with the strike until he pays us our money. We are not going to work.”
However, the HMB said the strike had not left the affected hospital departments without personnel.
An HMB source told Vanguard, “The various departments that are on strike, they have technicians, and the technicians are holding fort for them in the departments. There’s no vacuum.
“There are technicians—government-employed technicians—who are holding fort. There are pharmacy technicians, laboratory technicians and others.
“So, there’s no vacuum. Work is going on. My Permanent Secretary is even monitoring the situation.”
The Commissioner was yet to respond to the current impasse ahead of the renewed move for a truce meeting.

items.content:
Apple baru saja merilis update iOS 27 secara global pada 14 September 2026. Menariknya, pengguna iPhone 11 masih kebagian pembaruan ini. Selain iPhone 11, daftar resmi iPhone yang terima update iOS 27 ini juga mencakup iPhone SE generasi kedua.
Seperti biasa, perusahaan berbasis di Cupertino ini juga merilis iPadOS 27 hingga macOS 27 Golden Gate bersamaan dengan digulirkannya iOS 27.

Pengguna bisa langsung cek ketersediaan pembaruan lewat menu Pembaruan Software di iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, hingga Apple TV.
Sebelum mengunduh, cocokkan model perangkat dengan daftar berikut. Khusus MacBook, perhatikan chip yang digunakan karena tahun rilis saja belum cukup untuk memastikan dukungan.
Daftar iPhone yang Kebagian Update iOS 27
Mengutip keterangan di newsroom Apple, Selasa (15/9/2026), berikut adalah model iPhone yang kebagian iOS 27.
Daftar iPhone yang kompatibel antara lain:
KelompokModel yang mendukung iOS 27
iPhone terbaruiPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max
iPhone 17iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 17e
iPhone AiriPhone Air
iPhone 16iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e
iPhone 15iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max
iPhone 14iPhone 14, iPhone 14 Plus, iPhone 14 Pro, iPhone 14 Pro Max
iPhone 13iPhone 13, iPhone 13 mini, iPhone 13 Pro, iPhone 13 Pro Max
iPhone 12iPhone 12, iPhone 12 mini, iPhone 12 Pro, iPhone 12 Pro Max
iPhone 11iPhone 11, iPhone 11 Pro, iPhone 11 Pro Max
iPhone SEGenerasi kedua dan ketiga
Dapat iOS 27 Belum Tentu Dapat Seluruh Fitur AI
Ada perbedaan antara dukungan iOS dan persyaratan Apple Intelligence. iPhone yang bisa menjalankan iOS 27 belum tentu memenuhi syarat untuk fitur AI Apple.
Dalam panduan Apple Intelligence, Apple mencantumkan iPhone 15 Pro dan Pro Max serta model iPhone 16 atau lebih baru sebagai perangkat yang didukung. Ketersediaan fitur juga bergantung pada platform, bahasa, dan wilayah.
Artinya, pemilik iPhone 11 bisa memasang iOS 27, tetapi tidak otomatis mendapat Apple Intelligence. Hal serupa berlaku pada iPhone 15 dan iPhone 15 Plus.
Untuk iPad, persyaratan Apple Intelligence mencakup iPad mini dengan A17 Pro dan iPad berchip M1 atau lebih baru. Jadi, pisahkan daftar kompatibilitas sistem operasi dari syarat fitur AI saat memutuskan apa yang ingin dicoba.
Cara Download iOS 27 di iPhone
Buka aplikasi Settings > General > Software update
Jika iOS 18 sudah tersedia, klik tombol Download and Install.
Ikuti instruksi yang muncul di layar, dan tinggu hingga proses selesai.
Proses ini biasanya memakan waktu beberapa menit tergantung pada kecepatan internet dan model iPhone digunakan. Pastikan iPhone terhubung ke Wi-Fi dan baterainya lebih dari 50 persen untuk menghindari masalah selama proses update.
Fitur Baru iOS 27 Apa Saja?
Apple meluncurkan pembaruan perangkat lunak untuk iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, dan Apple TV. (Gizmologi/ Yuslianson)
Kecepatan menjadi salah satu sorotan di iOS 27 dan iPadOS 27. Apple mengklaim aplikasi bisa terbuka hingga 30 persen lebih cepat, foto yang baru diambil termuat hingga 70 persen lebih cepat, dan transfer AirDrop hingga 80 persen lebih cepat.
Di iPad, mencari file dan memindahkan file ke drive USB eksternal diklaim hingga lima kali lebih cepat, sebagaimana dikutip dari newsroom Apple, Selasa (15/9/2026).
Perusahaan berbasis di Cupertino itu juga memperbaiki respons jendela aplikasi saat ditutup, digeser, atau ketika pengguna berpindah dari satu jendela ke jendela lain.
Mac juga mendapat perbaikan serupa pada AirDrop dan penelusuran file jaringan. Unggahan Foto iCloud disebut mulai lebih cepat, sementara perpindahan antarruang kerja dan Mission Control dibuat lebih mulus.
Ada pula perubahan kecil  berguna saat koneksi lambat. Di aplikasi Pesan, pengguna tetap bisa mengirim balasan teks meski foto atau video berukuran besar masih dalam proses pengiriman.
Perpindahan antara Wi-Fi dan jaringan seluler di iPhone serta iPad juga diperbaiki agar koneksi beralih lebih lancar.
Tampilan Liquid Glass di iOS 27 Bisa Diatur
Sejak diperkenalkan pada iOS 26, Liquid Glass mengalami perubahan signifikan. Kini, Apple memberi pengguna lebih banyak kendali atas tampilan ini lewat slider baru di Pengaturan. 
Pengguna iPhone, iPad, hingga Mac kini bisa mengatur dengan lebih mudah tingkat kejernihan Liquid Glass dari sangat transparan hingga berwarna penuh.
Ikon aplikasi juga dipoles agar lebih tajam dan jelas. Sementara itu, pencarian di Spotlight, Foto, dan Mail diperbaiki agar pengguna lebih mudah menemukan informasi yang dicari.
Khusus Mail, sistem operasi baru Apple ini juga menempatkan hasil yang lebih relevan di bagian Hasil Teratas. Dengan begitu, pengguna bisa lebih cepat menemukan email yang sesuai dengan pencarian.
Berbagi foto turut mendapat perhatian. Album Bersama di iCloud kini mendukung foto dan video beresolusi penuh, sekaligus mempermudah pengguna Android dan Windows untuk bergabung serta menambahkan konten.
Orang Tua Bisa Atur Izin Akses Situs Anak
Kontrol Orang Tua di iOS 27
Untuk keluarga, Apple memperbarui pengaturan akun anak dan Durasi Layar. Orang tua bisa memilih aplikasi yang boleh digunakan sejak akun disiapkan, lalu menambah aplikasi secara bertahap.
Salah satu fitur baru adalah Minta Izin Penelusuran. Saat diaktifkan, anak harus mendapat persetujuan orang tua sebelum membuka situs baru di Safari.
Orang tua juga dapat menyetujui kontak baru yang akan terhubung dengan anak. Di sisi lain, Keamanan Komunikasi kini bisa mendeteksi dan memblokir konten sadis atau kekerasan dalam gambar serta video yang dibagikan.
Tampilan Durasi Layar dibuat lebih mudah dibaca. Orang tua bisa melihat rata-rata penggunaan perangkat dan aplikasi yang paling sering dipakai anak.
Batas waktu total harian dapat diatur untuk aplikasi Hiburan, Game, dan Media Sosial. Ada juga fitur Jadwal untuk menentukan aplikasi yang boleh dibuka pada jam tertentu.
Apple menyebut pengembangan pengaturan ini melibatkan panduan ahli klinis dan perkembangan anak. Panduan penggunaan tersedia melalui situs Keselamatan Anak Apple.
AirPods Dapat EQ, Apple TV Dukung Audio Lossless
Pembaruan Apple juga membawa EQ khusus untuk AirPods, sehingga pengguna bisa menyesuaikan karakter suara. Lewat perluasan Apple GymKit, pengguna AirPods Pro 3 dapat menyelaraskan data detak jantung melalui iPhone.
Di Apple Watch, musik disebut bisa mulai diputar lebih cepat. Saran widget Tumpukan Cerdas akan muncul saat relevan, dan widget bisa dibuka dengan gerakan ketuk satu tangan yang baru.
Apple TV mendapat dukungan audio lossless resolusi tinggi untuk Apple Music. Aplikasi Apple Podcasts tampil dengan desain baru, disertai pilihan ukuran teks yang lebih luas untuk aksesibilitas.
Aplikasi Kesehatan juga menambahkan dukungan perimenopause dan menopause pada Pelacakan Siklus, termasuk pemberitahuan penyimpangan siklus terkait perimenopause.
Sementara itu, Flyover di Peta Apple menggabungkan citra udara dengan AI untuk menampilkan detail visual yang lebih kaya.
Seluruh perubahan tersebut menjadi bagian dari pembaruan platform yang diumumkan Apple. Materi rilis yang dibagikan belum memerinci waktu distribusi untuk Indonesia.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By PAUL IBE
As Nigeria approaches the 2027 presidential election, much of the debate has centred on the qualifications, antecedents, integrity and eligibility of those seeking the presidency. But there is another question Nigerians should be asking: Are those seeking to lead Nigeria medically capable of discharging the enormous responsibilities of the presidency?
This is not about age, disability or stigmatising illness. It is not a licence for political persecution. It is a question of capacity, transparency and national security.
The 1999 Constitution, as amended, does not expressly require presidential candidates to undergo medical examinations. Yet it clearly recognises that medical incapacity can affect the ability to serve. Section 137 addresses unsoundness of mind, while Section 144 provides a constitutional procedure for determining whether a sitting President or Vice-President has become permanently incapable of performing the functions of office because of an infirmity of body or mind.
If the Constitution recognises medical incapacity as serious enough to potentially remove a sitting President, Nigerians are entitled to ask why there should be no credible mechanism for assessing presidential candidates before they are elected. Nigeria’s experience during the Buhari years demonstrated how presidential ill-health, prolonged medical absences and secrecy can generate enormous public anxiety and political controversy.
We should learn from that experience. The answer to speculation about a candidate’s health is not more speculation. It is independent professional assessment. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is seeking another term, and there has been considerable public discussion about his health. Even Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the ADC, alluded to that in a recent interview. But this should not become a Tinubu-only issue. If Tinubu is fit, let an independent panel establish it. If Atiku Abubakar is fit, let the same panel establish it. If Peter Obi is fit, let the same standard apply. And every other presidential candidate should be subjected to exactly the same process.
Medical fitness should also not be confused with physical perfection. A person can live productively with a chronic condition or disability and still be fully capable of serving as President. The relevant question is simple: Is the candidate medically capable of continuously and effectively discharging the constitutional responsibilities of the presidency?
The Nigerian Medical Association (NMA) should lead a national conversation on this issue. It has previously advocated medical and psychiatric evaluation of presidential and governorship candidates. An independent multidisciplinary panel could establish appropriate standards, conduct the assessments and provide a professional fitness certification while protecting legitimate medical privacy.
The presidency is not an ordinary occupation. The President is Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and bears enormous responsibility for national security, foreign policy and the direction of the Federal Government. Presidential health can therefore become a national-security question when it affects the capacity to perform those responsibilities.
The opposition should consequently demand a standard, not a diagnosis. Politicians should not attempt to diagnose candidates from photographs, speeches or social-media videos. Let qualified medical professionals determine fitness. Nigeria has spent enormous energy asking whether presidential candidates are legally qualified, politically popular or electorally viable. We should also ask whether they are medically capable of doing the job. Independent medical assessment. Equal standards. Professional certification. Appropriate transparency.
The time to establish that principle is before the 2027 election—not after another presidential health controversy becomes a national crisis.
•Ibe, Media Adviser to Atiku Abubakar, writes from Abuja.

By TUNDE RAHMAN
A fresh thaw in relations between National Democratic Congress presidential candidate Mr Peter Obi and Oyo State Governor Mr Seyi Makinde is fueling renewed talk of a possible opposition coalition to challenge President Bola Tinubu in 2027. The two leaders, who were on opposite sides during the 2023 election cycle, were seen together recently at a private meeting in Ibadan, Oyo State capital, followed by joint appearances at public events, including the inauguration of the Allied People’s Movement Presidential Campaign Office in Abuja last Monday. That campaign office belongs to Governor Makinde, a candidate in the race for the 2027 presidency on the APM platform.
The Obi-Makinde rapprochement comes after a plan by G-100, an amorphous group of opposition stakeholders advocating a united opposition front. Obi’s appearance at the inauguration of Makinde’s campaign office may be seen as raising the stakes in that plan. It was the first time in recent memory that a presidential candidate would appear at the opening of a campaign office of a rival candidate. Do the two have a working alliance, or is this just make-believe? Sources close to both camps say their discussions centred on “national interest, governance, and 2027 permutations.”
In 2023, Makinde, then a PDP chieftain, was part of the influential G-5 governors who worked against the then Peoples Democratic Party’s presidential candidate, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, while Obi led the Labour Party’s surprise third-force movement. Their paths diverged sharply on that 2023 campaign trail. But with four months to the January 16, 2027 presidential election, are the political realities forcing a rethink? The answer to the foregoing may only be conjectural. The big question, however, is whether opposition leaders can put their egos aside and present a united front in 2027.
In recent months, Governor Makinde has taken a more independent posture, often criticising federal policies while also calling for opposition unity. Wracked by an internal crisis within his PDP, he moved to the Allied People’s Movement to contest on its platform. Obi, on his part, has continued to mobilise his key support base under the “Obidient” movement and has not ruled out another presidential run. Can a potential Obi-Makinde alignment become the nucleus of a wider opposition front that may include aggrieved members of the PDP (not Wike’s PDP), Labour Party, NNPP, ADC, and other groups, along with NDC and APM? Can the seeming rapprochement move the opposition from fragmentation to coordination? Both Obi and Makinde have downplayed talk of a formal alliance, calling it “consultations among patriots.” Whether that produces a tangible result would depend on whether Obi, Makinde, and other opposition leaders, including the African Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, can bridge personal, regional, and party differences before the election season heats up.
Beyond handshakes and meetings, does the opposition actually have the numbers, structure, and unity to pose a real threat to President Tinubu and the APC? In my view, at least four factors are critical in deciding what happens. The first is the incumbency advantage. President Tinubu controls the awesome federal machinery. That lever means a lot. He has many achievements under the Renewed Hope Agenda that will work in his favour: improving and stabilising the economy with key positive indicators; many legacy roads and infrastructure projects; strategic federal appointments; student loans; the CrediCorp programme; and the CNG initiative, among others.
The “Renewed Hope Agenda: From Reforms to Prosperity” narrative is built on the bet that reforms will start showing tangible results now that the economy has stabilised. Lower food inflation, foreign exchange stability, and completed infrastructure projects will be the campaign touchpoints. The second and closely related point is that beating an incumbent in Nigeria is historically very hard. President Goodluck Jonathan, who was defeated by the APC coalition in 2015, is the only incumbent to have lost re-election in Nigeria’s history. And this was done by a coalition powered by the late President Muhammadu Buhari and President Tinubu. Can the opposition reenact 2015 in 2027? Third, party structure matters. The APC presently controls 31 states and has the largest grassroots party structure. Governors in the few other states not controlled by the party have declared support for President Tinubu’s re-election. These include Governors Chukwuma Soludo of Anambra State, in APGA; Labour Party’s Alex Otti of Abia; and Accord Party’s Ademola Adeleke of Osun State. Some in the opposition may scoff at this point, arguing that the people, not the governors, will decide. That still does not diminish the governors’ influence.
Lastly, the opposition’s new maths is confounding. According to them, Tinubu won the election with 37 per cent of the vote. That is the opposition’s opening line. They will then say: Atiku + Obi/Kwankwaso + Makinde will provide the theoretical numbers to defeat the incumbent. Yes, in 2023, the opposition parties ran separately, splitting the anti-APC vote, thus losing out and handing President Tinubu victory. In 2027, they must run together if they hope to pull off any surprise. This is easier said than done. Indeed, four big hurdles remain for an opposition coalition at this point, which can be categorised as reality/ambition/ego, zoning, formidable structure, and trust deficit. The reality is that Obi, Atiku, and now possibly Makinde all have presidential ambitions. They all have vaulting ambitions, and their egos are now at stake. Who steps down for whom? Who gets the vice-president’s slot?
And then there is the matter of zoning. The South wants to complete its eight years after the late President Buhari’s eight years. The North will argue that it is their turn soon again, possibly in 2031. A Northern candidate at this time may be swimming against the tide. Yet a Northern candidate promising one term in 2027 may be seen as short-changing the North. To succeed, a ticket must balance this critical issue, or it collapses. Forging a cohesive, formidable structure at this late hour, which is a difficult task, comes in again. And for Obi and Makinde, there could also be a trust deficit. The PDP and LP fought bitterly in 2023. Can party structures at the state level now integrate and work together in one day?
The Obi-Makinde alliance seems like a test. If they can agree on a framework and bring in more governors, the coalition becomes serious. If not, it remains mere optics. The 2027 election will not be won on personalities alone. It will also be won on some kitchen-table issues, of which the APC needs to be wary.
The elephant in the room is the cost of living. If food, transport, and electricity are still perceived as high by Q4 2026, “we did the hard part” may not move much. The opposition will run on “Tinubu made life harder,” which is what they want people to believe. Security is the other critical issue. The government and security agencies must maintain the present, apparently favourable security situation. Any major security breakdown in the North or Middle Belt will be weaponised. In the final analysis, the opposition can only pose a threat if three things happen. The first is one ticket. That is, a consensus presidential candidate emerges now, not later. Second, if some governors defect or align, the opposition will need at least eight to 10 governors to provide the structure and resources to make a big impact.
If those two things do not happen, President Tinubu wins again, likely with a bigger margin than in 2023, as the APC consolidates and the opposition remains fragmented. The Obi-Makinde rapprochement is not a coalition. It is a signal that opposition leaders know they lost in 2023 because they were divided. It signals that they are now testing the waters. Whether that signal becomes a threat depends on whether they can do what Nigerian politicians have failed to do for 25 years: put country and strategy ahead of personal ambition. President Tinubu is the favourite. But for the first time since 2023, the APC may now have something to worry about.
•Rahman is Senior Special Assistant to President Tinubu on Media & Special Duties.

tags: On the Spot with Eric Teniola
items.content:
This week, we continue the series on why the House of Chiefs should be considered by the National Assembly.
He was labour officer, Federal Ministry of Labour, Lagos, 1962–1963; lecturer, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, 1963–1965; assistant professor of political science, California, 1969–1971; associate professor of African Studies, University of Maryland, Baltimore, Maryland, USA, 1972–1974; dean of studies, Institute of Management and Technology, Enugu, 1974–1976; and appointed director, National Policy Development Centre, May 1976.
Mazi Samuel Goomsu Ikoku was a Nigerian trade unionist and politician. As a student at the University of Southampton, Ikoku supported Nigeria’s independence movement, writing articles printed by the West African Pilot. After his degree, he joined the radical arm of the independence movement, working as an adviser to the Nigerian Federation of Labour led by Michael Imoudu and later co-founding the United Working People’s Party in 1952. A year later, the party was officially disbanded by the government after being branded subversive and communist. Ikoku later began a relationship with the Action Group (AG) that spanned the majority of the First Republic.
Mazi Ikoku sometimes spoke on national issues with a sense of candor; this style led to him being called a controversial figure by former Science and Technology Minister Sam Momah.
Ikoku graduated from Achimota College and later studied at University College, Southampton. Beginning in 1946, Ikoku took interest in the independence movement led by Nnamdi Azikiwe. He began writing articles in Azikiwe’s West African Pilot criticizing the Legislative Council, in which his father was a nominated member, arguing against the council as an imposed government and aligning with Azikiwe’s ideas about immediate independence.
While studying he met his future spouse, Eileen. He returned to Nigeria in 1949 and joined the civil service; during this time, he took up advisory roles with trade unions in the country. He left government work in 1951 to dedicate his time to the Nigerian Federation of Labour, which was seeking affiliation with the World Federation of Trade Unions.
Mazi Ikoku also joined a group of young socialists to form a short-lived political organization, the United Working People’s Party, independent of prominent individuals. During this time, he began publishing a journal with editorials supporting Stalinist ideas. Both the journal and the paper were disbanded by colonial authorities.
In the 1950s, Mazi Ikoku joined one of the mainstream parties when he became a member of the Action Group, which then had a strong organizational structure. Ikoku was immediately given the position of organizing secretary. In 1957, he won a regional House of Assembly election; in the assembly he represented the AG and served as the leader of the opposition. During the campaigns preceding the election, Ikoku’s father was contesting the same seat under the United National Independent Party. 
Mazi Ikoku was a member of the Action Group’s socialist faction. This faction was to focus on ideology as a political campaign tool and believed in imperialism as a pressing danger. In 1960, the party adopted democratic socialism as an ideology, but the party’s national executive and the Western regional premier leaned towards capitalism.
In 1962, he traveled to Ghana days before the factional crisis engulfed the Western Region House of Assembly, leading to a state of emergency. Some factional members of the Action Group were later charged with treason. In Ghana, Ikoku organized a branch of the party and also worked as a lecturer at Nkrumah’s Ideological Institute and as an editor for the Spark magazine, published in Ghana.
During the Nigerian Civil War, Mazi Ikoku did not support secession. He was briefly detained after his return from Ghana but was later appointed commissioner for Economic Development and later Health in the East Central State.
Mazi Ikoku broke ranks with former Action Group members and joined Aminu Kano’s People’s Redemption Party during the Second Republic. He was appointed Secretary-General of the party, which believed in the emancipation of the talakawa. He was Aminu Kano’s running mate in the 1979 presidential election, which was won by Shehu Shagari. However, beginning during the twilight of the republic, Ikoku began to shift away from his socialist ideas. He left the PRP and became an adviser to Shehu Shagari of the National Party of Nigeria.
He spoke of elongating the role of the military in Nigeria’s political affairs during the administration of Ibrahim Babangida and later served as deputy chairman of the Transition Implementation Committee during Sani Abacha’s regime. As deputy chairman, Mazi Ikoku argued that Abacha was free to succeed himself if the political parties agreed to draft him as their presidential candidate.
He died in 1997. Mazi Ikoku was the stepfather of Patti Boulaye.
Professor Godwin Anibeze Odenigwe was born on December 12, 1925. He had his education at the Central School, Umabi, 1931–1932; St. Patrick’s School, Amokwe, 1937–1940; St. Thomas School, Udi, 1941; St. Charles Teacher Training College, Onitsha, 1942–1945; Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia, USA, 1950–1953; Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, USA, 1953–1957; University of London, England; called to the bar, Gray’s Inn, London, 1958; senior lecturer and head, Department of Government and Administration, Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology, Ibadan; senior lecturer and head, Department of Political Science, University of Nigeria, Nsukka; reader in political science, later professor of political science, University of Nigeria; and special adviser to the President for Political Affairs, 1979–1983.

items.content:
“Can Education Survive Attack: The Resilience of Human Communities” is the theme of this year’s International Day to Protect Education from Attack, marked on 9 September. This is very apt for Nigeria as schools reopen for the 2026/2027 session. For a country where children are abducted from schools, the occasion is a painful reminder of a national failure. A government that cannot guarantee the safety of children in classrooms and hostels is failing one of its most fundamental responsibilities.
Schools are sanctuaries of learning, not hunting grounds for terrorists and bandits who exploit pupils and teachers for ransom, propaganda, and psychological warfare. The Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack recorded at least 8,566 attacks on education worldwide in 2024 and 2025, more than a 40 per cent increase over the preceding two-year period. The attacks harmed at least 10,600 students, teachers, and education personnel. Nigeria’s experience gives this global crisis a particularly painful meaning.
In Askira-Uba LGA of Borno State, only 56 of 113 primary schools were functioning as of late August 2026, while about 80 students abducted during attacks in May and June remained in captivity. In several vulnerable communities, insecurity has forced schools to close altogether. The country has not forgotten Chibok, Dapchi, or Kankara. Yet the attacks continue. On 17 November 2025, gunmen abducted 25 schoolgirls from the Government Girls Comprehensive Secondary School in Maga, Kebbi State, after killing the vice-principal. Four days later, 303 students and 12 teachers were abducted from St Mary’s Catholic School in Papiri, Niger State. These were evidence of a persistent failure to secure vulnerable learning environments.
Parents become afraid to send their children to school. Teachers resist postings to vulnerable communities. Schools close, learning is disrupted, and some children never return. UNICEF has warned that attacks on schools and abduction of teachers and pupils are causing frequent closures and preventing hundreds of thousands of Nigerian children from receiving consistent education. Nigeria endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration in May 2015 and subsequently developed a National Policy on Safety, Security and Violence-Free Schools. These are valuable commitments, but declarations and policies cannot protect a single child without implementation.
The government must provide adequate physical protection for vulnerable schools, intelligence-led surveillance, emergency communication systems, and rapid-response mechanisms. Communities must be integrated into security arrangements, while boarding schools in high-risk areas require special protection, controlled access, and regularly tested evacuation plans. Education is not a luxury that can wait until Nigeria becomes secure. It is actually a strong national security instrument. Every school closed by terrorists or bandits is a victory for those who want Nigeria’s children uneducated, impoverished, and vulnerable. 
The government must see the protection of education as beyond an education-sector responsibility. Budgets, intelligence, security deployment, and emergency preparedness must reflect that priority.
